question_text: A pharmacopoeial monograph includes all of the following EXCEPT:
explanation: A pharmacopoeial monograph includes name, molecular formula, method of preparation, physical/chemical properties, identification tests, purity tests, assay, storage, and uses — not drug price.

question_text: According to the Brønsted-Lowry concept, an acid is defined as:
explanation: According to the Brønsted-Lowry concept, an acid is a proton (H+) donor and a base is a proton acceptor.

question_text: Boric acid is used as:
explanation: Boric acid is used as a mild antiseptic, particularly as an eye wash (1-4% solution) and for minor skin infections. It is not used systemically due to toxicity.

question_text: Sodium benzoate is primarily used as:
explanation: Sodium benzoate is a widely used preservative in pharmaceutical and food products. It is effective in acidic media (pH below 4.5) where it converts to benzoic acid.

question_text: BHA and BHT are classified as:
explanation: Butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA) and butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT) are synthetic antioxidants used to prevent oxidative degradation of fats and oils in pharmaceutical preparations.

question_text: Aluminum hydroxide gel is classified as:
explanation: Aluminum hydroxide gel is an antacid that neutralizes gastric acid. It also has absorbent properties. It may cause constipation, so it is often combined with magnesium hydroxide.

question_text: Magnesium trisilicate acts as an antacid by:
options: Inhibiting the proton pump present in the gastric parietal cells
Neutralizing gastric acid and protecting the gastric mucosa
Stimulating the smooth muscle of the stomach to speed up gastric emptying
Blocking histamine at H2 receptors located in the stomach wall
explanation:
Magnesium trisilicate neutralizes gastric acid and forms a protective coating of hydrated magnesium silicate over the gastric mucosa.

Additional: forming a protective coating

question_text: Magnesium sulphate is used as:
options: An antacid that neutralizes hydrochloric acid in the stomach
An emollient that softens and soothes the skin
An astringent that precipitates proteins on the skin surface
explanation: Magnesium sulphate (Epsom salt) is used as a purgative laxative. When taken orally, it draws water into the intestine osmotically, promoting bowel movements.

question_text: Calamine is primarily used as:
options: An internal antiseptic taken by mouth for gut infections
An astringent used alone to dry and harden the skin
An antifungal agent applied for ringworm infections
explanation: Calamine (zinc oxide with ferric oxide) is used as a protective agent and for its anti-pruritic (anti-itch) properties in skin conditions like sunburn, insect bites, and poison ivy.

question_text: Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) acts as an antimicrobial agent by:
explanation: Hydrogen peroxide releases nascent oxygen (O) upon contact with catalase in tissues, which is a powerful oxidizing agent that kills microorganisms.

question_text: Sodium fluoride is used in dentistry as:
explanation: Sodium fluoride is used as an anti-caries agent. It incorporates into tooth enamel forming fluorapatite, which is more resistant to acid demineralization.

question_text: Ammonium chloride is used as:
explanation: Ammonium chloride is used as an expectorant. It irritates the gastric mucosa reflexly increasing respiratory tract secretions, helping to thin mucus.

question_text: Activated charcoal is used as an antidote because it:
options: Neutralizes stomach acids by direct chemical reaction
Adsorbs toxins in the GI tract
Kills the bacteria present in the gut by direct action
Promotes vomiting to expel the poison from the stomach
explanation: Activated charcoal has a large surface area that adsorbs most ingested toxins and drugs in the GI tract, preventing their absorption into the bloodstream.

question_text: Ferrous fumarate is classified as a:
explanation:
Ferrous fumarate is a hematinic agent used to treat and prevent iron-deficiency anemia. It provides iron for hemoglobin synthesis.

Note: antianemic

question_text: ORS (Oral Rehydration Salts) contain primarily:
options: Calcium carbonate and ferrous sulphate as the main electrolytes
Only glucose in a concentrated sugar solution
Only sodium chloride dissolved in sterile water
explanation:
ORS contains sodium chloride, potassium chloride, glucose (or glycine), and trisodium citrate (or sodium bicarbonate) to replace water and electrolytes lost in diarrheal dehydration.

Note: glucose, and sodium citrate

question_text: Ringer Lactate solution is used for:
options: Oral rehydration after acute diarrheal illness
Irrigation of the eye after a chemical injury
Cleaning of open wounds before application of a dressing
explanation: Ringer Lactate (Hartmann's solution) is an intravenous crystalloid solution used for fluid and electrolyte replacement, particularly in burns, surgery, and dehydration.

question_text: Barium sulphate is used as:
options: An internal contrast medium for visualizing the stomach on plain X-ray
Radio-opaque contrast media for GI imaging
A radioactive isotope that emits gamma rays for imaging the thyroid
An antacid that neutralizes excess acid in the stomach
explanation: Barium sulphate is used as a radio-opaque contrast medium for imaging the gastrointestinal tract (barium meal, barium swallow). It is not absorbed from the GI tract.

question_text: The limit test for chloride is based on the reaction of chloride ions with:
explanation:
The limit test for chloride involves the reaction of chloride ions with silver nitrate in the presence of dilute nitric acid to form a white precipitate of silver chloride (AgCl).

Additional: white precipitate of AgCl

question_text: A primary standard should have all EXCEPT:
explanation: A primary standard should NOT be hygroscopic. It should have high purity, stability in air, non-toxicity, high molecular weight, and be readily available at low cost.

question_text: 1 M (Molar) solution contains:
explanation: A 1 M (molar) solution contains 1 mole of solute dissolved in 1 litre of solution. Molarity (M) = moles of solute / litres of solution.

question_text: In an acid-base titration, methyl orange indicator changes color from:
explanation:
Methyl orange changes color from red (in acid, pH < 3.1) to yellow (in base, pH > 4.4). It is used as an indicator in strong acid-weak base titrations.

Note: or vice versa

question_text: Iodometry involves:
explanation: Iodometry is an indirect (back) titration method where iodine is liberated by reaction with an oxidizing agent, and the liberated iodine is titrated with standardized sodium thiosulphate solution.

question_text: Column chromatography separates compounds based on:
options: Differences in the molecular weights of the components
Differential adsorption of components on the stationary phase
Differences in the boiling points of the components
Differences in the densities of the components
explanation:
Column chromatography separates compounds based on differential adsorption. Components with weaker adsorption to the stationary phase elute first, while strongly adsorbed components elute later.

Additional: and mobile phase

question_text: HPLC stands for:
explanation: HPLC stands for High Performance Liquid Chromatography. It is an analytical technique used for separating, identifying, and quantifying components in a mixture.

question_text: Bronsted-Lowry acid is a:
explanation: A Bronsted-Lowry acid is a substance that donates a proton (H+).

question_text: Sodium bicarbonate is used as:
explanation: Sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) is an antacid that neutralizes stomach acid and can also be used as a buffering agent.

question_text: Buffer capacity depends on:
options: The pH of the buffer solution alone
The atmospheric pressure at which the buffer solution is stored
The total volume of buffer solution that has been prepared
explanation:
Buffer capacity depends on the absolute concentrations of buffer components and the ratio of acid to conjugate base.

Additional: and their ratio

question_text: Sodium metabisulphite is used as:
explanation: Sodium metabisulphite is a common antioxidant used to prevent oxidation in pharmaceutical preparations.

question_text: Methylparaben is classified as:
explanation: Methylparaben (and propylparaben) are antimicrobial preservatives used to prevent microbial growth in formulations.

question_text: Aluminum hydroxide gel is used as:
explanation: Al(OH)3 is a non-systemic antacid that neutralizes gastric acid and has a constipating effect.

question_text: Magnesium hydroxide has:
explanation: Mg(OH)2 (milk of magnesia) has an osmotic laxative effect, drawing water into the intestine.

question_text: Magnesium trisilicate is used as:
options: Antacid with slow and prolonged action
Analgesic for mild to moderate pain
explanation: Magnesium trisilicate acts as a slow, prolonged-acting antacid by reacting with HCl to form MgCl2 and silicic acid.

question_text: Light kaolin is used as:
options: Analgesic for mild to moderate pain
explanation: Light kaolin is an adsorbent that adsorbs toxins and bacteria in diarrhea, providing protective and adsorbent action.

question_text: Calcium carbonate is an:
explanation: CaCO3 is a non-systemic antacid that also serves as a dietary calcium supplement.

question_text: Zinc oxide is used as:
options: Protective and mild astringent for skin
explanation: Zinc oxide is a protective and mild astringent used in ointments, pastes, and dusting powders for skin protection.

question_text: Calamine is:
options: A medicine taken by mouth to treat internal infections
An injectable solution given intravenously for electrolyte balance
An oral suspension used to treat cough and cold symptoms
explanation: Calamine (zinc oxide with iron oxide) is a protective and antipruritic preparation used for skin irritations.

question_text: Povidone iodine is classified as:
explanation:
Povidone iodine is a broad-spectrum antimicrobial agent effective against bacteria, fungi, viruses, and spores.

Note: broad-spectrum

question_text: Talc is used in pharmacy as:
explanation: Talc (Mg3Si4O10(OH)2) is a very fine, soft mineral used as a protective dusting powder and tablet dusting agent.

question_text: Silver nitrate is used as:
explanation: AgNO3 is used as a caustic agent (for warts) and antimicrobial (prophylaxis of neonatal ophthalmia).

question_text: Activated charcoal is used as:
options: An antacid that neutralizes excess acid secreted in the stomach
A stimulant laxative used to relieve chronic constipation
An analgesic used to relieve mild to moderate pain
explanation: Activated charcoal has a large surface area that adsorbs most ingested poisons, used as an emergency antidote.

question_text: Ferrous fumarate is a:
explanation:
Ferrous fumarate is an iron preparation used to treat and prevent iron deficiency anemia.

Note: iron supplement for anemia

question_text: ORS contains all EXCEPT:
explanation: ORS contains NaCl, KCl, glucose, and trisodium citrate. It does NOT contain CaCl2.

question_text: Calcium gluconate is used for:
explanation:
Calcium gluconate treats hypocalcemia and is an antidote for hyperkalemia (protects the heart).

Additional: hyperkalemia emergency

question_text: Potassium chloride supplements are given for:
explanation:
KCl supplements treat hypokalemia, which can occur from diuretic use or poor dietary intake.

Note: low potassium

question_text: Sodium bicarbonate is used in:
explanation: NaHCO3 is used to treat metabolic acidosis by buffering excess acid and raising blood pH.

question_text: In acid-base titration, the endpoint is:
options: The point where moles of acid equal moles of base
The point where indicator changes color
explanation: The endpoint is the point at which the indicator changes color, ideally matching the equivalence point.

question_text: Molarity is defined as:
options: Grams of solute per liter of solution
Moles of solute per liter of solution
Moles of solute per kg of solvent
explanation: Molarity (M) = moles of solute / liters of solution. It is the most commonly used concentration unit in pharmacy.

question_text: Phenolphthalein changes color in the range:
explanation: Phenolphthalein is colorless below pH 8.2 and pink above pH 10, used as an indicator in strong acid-strong base titrations.

question_text: Iodometric titration involves:
options: Direct titration of the sample with a standard solution of iodine
Titration of liberated iodine with sodium thiosulfate
Titration of the sample with a standard solution of chlorine water
Titration of the sample with a standard solution of bromine water
explanation: Iodometric titration involves liberating iodine from iodide by an oxidizing agent, then titrating the liberated iodine with Na2S2O3.

question_text: In column chromatography, the mobile phase is called:
explanation: The mobile phase (eluent) moves through the stationary phase, carrying components at different rates for separation.

question_text: Rf value in TLC is:
options: Ratio of solvent front to spot
Distance moved by solute / distance moved by solvent front
Distance travelled by the solvent front alone on the plate
explanation: Rf = distance moved by solute / distance moved by solvent front. Rf values help identify compounds in TLC.

question_text: Limit test for chloride involves:
options: Titration of the sample with a standard solution of silver nitrate
Formation of white turbidity with silver
Measuring the intensity of color produced with a chromogenic reagent
Weighing the precipitate formed after adding dilute nitric acid
explanation:
Chloride limit test: add dilute HNO3 and AgNO3. White turbidity indicates chloride; compare with standard turbidity.

Additional: nitrate in dilute nitric acid

question_text: Limit test for sulphate uses:
explanation: Sulphate limit test: add dilute HCl and BaCl2. White turbidity of BaSO4 indicates sulphate presence.

question_text: Identification test for iron involves:
explanation:
Iron is identified by adding ammonium thiocyanate, which forms a deep blood-red colored complex with Fe3+ ions.

Additional: producing blood-red color

question_text: Melting point determination is used for:
options: Measuring the analgesic potency of the substance being tested
Testing whether the substance is sterile or contaminated
Measuring the pH of the substance in aqueous solution
explanation:
Melting point indicates purity (impurities lower the melting point) and helps identify solid crystalline drugs.

Additional: of solid drugs

question_text: Precision in analytical chemistry refers to:
explanation:
Precision is the reproducibility/closeness of repeated measurements to each other, independent of accuracy.

Additional: to each other

question_text: What is pharmaceutical chemistry?

options.a: Study of drug prices
options.b: The branch of chemistry
options.c: Study of drug packaging
options.d: Study of drug marketing

explanation:
Pharmaceutical chemistry combines organic chemistry, medicinal chemistry, and analytical chemistry for drug design, synthesis, and quality evaluation.

Note: synthesis, and quality control of pharmaceutical drugs

Additional: concerned with design development
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is medicinal chemistry?

options.a: The study of how medicines are compounded and dispensed in a pharmacy
options.b: The application of chemical knowledge to drug design and discovery
options.c: The science of measuring drug concentrations in samples of body fluids
options.d: The art of preparing tablets, capsules and syrups on an industrial scale

explanation: Medicinal chemistry involves designing and synthesizing new drugs, understanding structure-activity relationships (SAR), and optimizing drug molecules for therapeutic use.
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a functional group in organic chemistry?

options.a: A group of atoms that has a fixed atomic mass and charge
options.b: A specific group of atoms within a molecule that determines reactivity
options.c: A type of atom that carries a fixed ionic charge in all compounds
options.d: A chemical bond formed between two carbon atoms in a chain

explanation:
Functional groups are reactive groups that determine the chemical properties and reactions of organic molecules (e.g., -OH, -COOH, -NH2, -CHO).

Additional: molecule responsible for characteristic chemical reactions
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: Which functional group is present in alcohols?

options.a: -COOH
options.b: -OH
options.c: -CHO
options.d: -NH2

explanation:
Alcohols contain the hydroxyl (-OH) group attached to a carbon atom. Examples: ethanol (CH3CH2OH), methanol (CH3OH).

Note: hydroxyl
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: Which functional group is present in carboxylic acids?

options.a: -OH
options.b: -CHO
options.c: -COOH
options.d: -CO-

explanation:
Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group (-COOH), which is acidic. Examples: acetic acid (CH3COOH), benzoic acid (C6H5COOH).

Note: carboxyl
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the IUPAC name of aspirin?

options.a: Acetylsalicylic acid
options.b: 2-Acetoxybenzoic acid
options.c: Salicylic acid
options.d: Acetic acid

explanation: Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid, IUPAC name: 2-acetoxybenzoic acid. It is synthesized by acetylation of salicylic acid with acetic anhydride.
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the chemical formula of paracetamol (acetaminophen)?

options.a: C8H9NO2
options.b: C9H8O4
options.c: C7H6O3
options.d: C10H12N2O

explanation: Paracetamol (N-acetyl-p-aminophenol) has the formula C8H9NO2. It is synthesized by acetylation of p-aminophenol with acetic anhydride.
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the chemical name of paracetamol?

options.a: Acetylsalicylic acid
options.b: N-acetamide
options.c: 2-Acetoxybenzoic acid
options.d: 4-Aminophenol

explanation: Paracetamol is N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetamide (N-acetyl-p-aminophenol). The hydroxyl group is para to the acetamide group on the benzene ring.
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the synthesis of aspirin?

options.a: Reaction of salicylic acid with ethanol in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid
options.b: Acetylation of salicylic acid with acetic anhydride in presence of H2SO4
options.c: Reaction of phenol with acetic acid to form the ester directly
options.d: Oxidation of benzoic acid with potassium permanganate in alkaline medium

explanation: Aspirin is synthesized by reacting salicylic acid with acetic anhydride in the presence of a catalyst (H2SO4 or H3PO4) to produce acetylsalicylic acid and acetic acid.
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the role of H2SO4 in aspirin synthesis?

options.a: It is a reactant
options.b: It acts as a catalyst
options.c: It purifies the product
options.d: It neutralizes the product

explanation:
Concentrated H2SO4 acts as an acid catalyst, protonating the carbonyl oxygen of acetic anhydride, making it more electrophilic and facilitating attack by the hydroxyl group of salicylic acid.

Note: proton donor

Additional: to facilitate the acetylation reaction
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the theory of drug action?

options.a: A theory of how drug prices are fixed in the pharmaceutical market
options.b: Mechanisms by which drugs interact with receptors
options.c: A description of the manufacturing process used to produce the drug
options.d: A description of the methods used to distribute drugs to pharmacies

explanation:
Drug action theory explains how drugs interact with receptors, enzymes, ion channels, and transporters to produce pharmacological effects.

Additional: biological systems to produce therapeutic effects
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a pharmacophore?

options.a: The total number of functional groups present in a drug molecule
options.b: The minimum structural features required in a molecule for biological activity at a target receptor
options.c: The metabolic pathway by which a drug is inactivated in the liver
options.d: The site where a drug is stored after it has been absorbed into the body

explanation:
A pharmacophore is the essential 3D arrangement of functional groups necessary for a drug to interact with its biological target. It guides drug design and SAR studies.

Additional: for biological activity at a target receptor
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is structure-activity relationship (SAR)?

options.a: Drug structure and its price
options.b: The relationship between a drug's chemical
options.c: Drug structure and packaging
options.d: Drug structure and taste

explanation:
SAR studies how modifications to a drug's chemical structure affect its potency, selectivity, toxicity, and pharmacokinetics, guiding the design of better drugs.

Additional: structure and its biological activity
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a lead compound?

options.a: A heavy metal compound like lead oxide
options.b: A compound with known biological activity that serves
options.c: A final drug product ready for market
options.d: An inactive compound with no activity

explanation:
A lead compound is a molecule with demonstrated pharmacological activity that serves as the starting point for optimization through chemical modification to improve potency and reduce toxicity.

Additional: as a starting point for drug development
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is bioisosterism?

options.a: The study of how the same biochemical reactions occur in different species
options.b: Replacement of an atom or group with a similar one
options.c: The study of identical biochemical pathways operating in all organisms
options.d: The use of the same test organism for studying all drug reactions

explanation:
Bioisosteric replacement substitutes atoms/groups with similar physicochemical properties (e.g., replacing -H with -F, -OH with -NH2) to optimize drug activity, metabolism, or bioavailability.

Note: similar size/shape/electronics

Additional: bioisostere to modify drug properties without losing activity
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a prodrug?

options.a: A drug that is always administered by the intravenous route
options.b: An inactive compound that is converted to an active drug in the body
options.c: A drug that is given before surgery to prepare the patient
options.d: A drug that is used only to prevent disease rather than treat it

explanation:
Prodrugs are pharmacologically inactive compounds that undergo biotransformation (metabolism) in vivo to release the active drug. They improve bioavailability, taste, or reduce side effects.

Additional: active drug in the body by metabolic processes
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: Give an example of a prodrug.

options.a: Aspirin
options.b: Enalapril
options.c: Paracetamol
options.d: Caffeine

explanation:
Enalapril is an ethyl ester prodrug hydrolyzed to enalaprilat (active ACE inhibitor). Other examples: levodopa (to dopamine), codeine (to morphine), valacyclovir (to acyclovir).

Note: converted to enalaprilat
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the difference between a drug and a medicine?

options.a: A drug is the finished formulation while a medicine is the raw chemical compound
options.b: A drug is a chemical substance; a medicine is a drug in a suitable dosage form
options.c: A medicine is always given by injection while a drug is always taken by mouth
options.d: A substance becomes a medicine only when it is obtained from a plant source

explanation:
A drug is any chemical substance that affects biological function. A medicine is a finished pharmaceutical product containing the drug plus excipients in a suitable dosage form.

Additional: a drug formulated for therapeutic use with excipients

Note: a medicine is
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is an excipient?

options.a: The pharmacologically active ingredient that produces the therapeutic effect
options.b: An inactive substance added to a pharmaceutical formulation as a carrier or filler
options.c: A toxic metabolite of the drug that must be monitored during therapy
options.d: An impurity that must be completely removed during tablet manufacturing

explanation:
Excipients are inactive ingredients in a pharmaceutical product: fillers (lactose), binders (PVP), disintegrants (starch), lubricants (magnesium stearate), preservatives, etc.

Note: or for other technical purposes

Additional: pharmaceutical formulation as a carrier filler
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the difference between a pure substance and a mixture?

options.a: A pure substance always exists in the liquid state at room temperature
options.b: A pure substance has a fixed composition; a mixture has variable composition
options.c: A pure substance can be separated into its components by simple physical methods
options.d: A mixture always boils at one fixed temperature like a pure compound

explanation:
A pure substance (compound/element) has a definite chemical composition. A mixture (solution, suspension) contains components that can be separated physically.

Additional: mixture contains two or more substances physically combined

Note: a mixture does not
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the pH scale?

options.a: A scale for measuring drug potency
options.b: A logarithmic scale measuring the acidity
options.c: A temperature scale
options.d: A pressure measurement

explanation:
pH = -log[H+]. pH 7 is neutral, pH < 7 is acidic, pH > 7 is alkaline. Most drugs are weak acids or bases, and their ionization depends on pH.

Note: 0-14

Additional: or alkalinity of a solution
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a buffer solution?

options.a: A solution whose pH changes markedly on adding a few drops of acid
options.b: A solution that resists pH change when small amounts of acid or base are added
options.c: A solution prepared by dissolving a single salt in pure distilled water
options.d: A solution that always maintains a pH of exactly 7 regardless of what is added

explanation:
Buffers consist of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base and conjugate acid). They maintain stable pH, important in pharmaceutical formulations and biological systems.

Additional: small amounts of acid or base are added
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a salt in pharmaceutical chemistry?

options.a: A covalent compound formed by sharing electrons between two nonmetal atoms
options.b: An ionic compound formed from the reaction of an acid with a base
options.c: A compound that releases hydroxide ions when dissolved in water
options.d: An oxide of a metal that dissolves in water to give an alkaline solution

explanation:
Pharmaceutical salts (e.g., sodium salicylate, hydrochloride salts of alkaloids) are formed to improve water solubility, stability, and bioavailability of drugs.

Additional: with a base often used to improve drug solubility
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: Why are drugs often converted to salt forms?

options.a: To improve the taste of the drug so that patients accept it readily
options.b: To improve water solubility, dissolution rate
options.c: To increase the selling price of the finished pharmaceutical product
options.d: To eliminate all of the side effects of the drug completely

explanation:
Salt formation improves aqueous solubility (essential for absorption), dissolution rate, chemical stability, crystallinity, and manufacturing properties.

Note: stability, and bioavailability
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the difference between a racemic mixture and an enantiopure compound?

options.a: A racemic mixture rotates plane-polarized light just as strongly as each pure enantiomer
options.b: A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of both enantiomers
options.c: A racemic mixture is always less soluble in water than the individual enantiomers
options.d: An enantiopure compound has physical properties identical to those of the racemic mixture

explanation:
A racemic mixture (50:50) contains both mirror-image enantiomers. An enantiopure compound contains only one enantiomer (e.g., S-omeprazole = esomeprazole).

Additional: enantiomers; an enantiopure compound contains only one enantiomer
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is chirality in drug molecules?

options.a: The color a drug solution produces when it is exposed to plane-polarized light
options.b: The property of a molecule having non-superimposable mirror images like left and right hands
options.c: The ease with which a drug dissolves in water at body temperature
options.d: The resistance of a drug to chemical breakdown during long-term storage

explanation:
Chirality means a molecule exists as two mirror-image forms (enantiomers). Drug enantiomers can have different pharmacological activities (e.g., S-ibuprofen is active, R is inactive).

Additional: mirror images like left and right hands
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: Give an example where drug enantiomers have different activities.

options.a: Aspirin enantiomers are identical
options.b: Thalidomide:
options.c: Paracetamol enantiomers are different
options.d: Caffeine has no enantiomers

explanation:
Thalidomide's S-enantiomer causes birth defects while R-enantiomer is sedative. In vivo, they interconvert. Other examples: S-naproxen (active), S-omeprazole (esomeprazole, more potent).

Note: R-enantiomer is sedative; S-enantiomer is teratogenic
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a functional group interconversion (FGI)?

options.a: Changing the brand of a drug
options.b: Chemical transformation of one functional group
options.c: Changing the dose of a drug
options.d: Changing the dosage form of a drug

explanation:
FGI involves converting one functional group to another (e.g., -OH to -Cl, -COOH to -COOR) as a step in drug synthesis or to modify drug properties.

Additional: into another during drug synthesis
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is nucleophilic substitution?

options.a: A reaction where a nucleophile attacks an electrophilic carbon
options.b: A process in which the nucleus of the atom itself is replaced by another nucleus
options.c: An addition reaction in which a reagent adds across a carbon-carbon double bond
options.d: An elimination reaction in which water is removed from an alcohol molecule

explanation:
In nucleophilic substitution, a nucleophile (electron-rich species like OH-, NH2-, Cl-) attacks an electrophilic carbon, displacing a leaving group (SN1 or SN2 mechanism).

Additional: electrophilic carbon replacing a leaving group
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the difference between SN1 and SN2 reactions?

options.a: No difference
options.b: SN1 is two-step; SN2 is one-step
options.c: SN1 is faster
options.d: SN2 gives racemic products

explanation:
SN1: stepwise, rate depends on substrate only, goes through carbocation, gives racemization. SN2: concerted, rate depends on substrate and nucleophile, backside attack, gives inversion.

Note: backside attack, inversion of configuration

Note: via carbocation, racemization
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is an esterification reaction?

options.a: Making an ester from an alcohol and an acid
options.b: Breaking an ester into acid and alcohol
options.c: Oxidation of an alcohol
options.d: Reduction of a carboxylic acid

explanation:
Esterification (Fischer esterification) is the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol in acid catalyst to form an ester and water. It is used in prodrug design.

Note: or acid chloride/anhydride
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is hydrolysis in pharmaceutical chemistry?

options.a: Adding water to split a molecule into two parts
options.b: A reaction with water that breaks chemical bonds in a drug molecule
options.c: Dissolving a drug in water
options.d: Evaporating water from a solution

explanation: Hydrolysis is the cleavage of chemical bonds by water. Many drugs (esters, amides, lactams) undergo hydrolysis, which can be a route of drug metabolism or degradation.
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is an amide bond (peptide bond)?

options.a: A covalent bond formed by sharing electrons between two carbon atoms in an alkane
options.b: A -CO-NH- linkage formed between a carboxylic acid and an amine, with loss of a water molecule
options.c: A bond between two nitrogen atoms formed by the loss of a hydrogen molecule
options.d: The O-H covalent bond that is present in every alcohol and phenol molecule

explanation:
The amide (peptide) bond -CO-NH- is formed by condensation of a carboxylic acid and an amine. It is planar, rigid (partial double bond character), and forms the backbone of proteins and peptides.

Additional: and an amine the backbone of proteins
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is oxidation in organic chemistry?

options.a: Adding hydrogen
options.b: Loss of electrons or gain of oxygen
options.c: Adding water
options.d: Breaking bonds with water

explanation:
Oxidation involves loss of electrons, gain of oxygen, or loss of hydrogen. Primary alcohols oxidize to aldehydes then carboxylic acids; secondary alcohols to ketones.

Additional: oxygen/loss of hydrogen from a molecule
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is reduction in organic chemistry?

options.a: Loss of electrons from, or loss of hydrogen by, an organic molecule
options.b: Gain of electrons or gain of hydrogen
options.c: Combination of a substance with oxygen or the loss of hydrogen from it
options.d: Removal of a water molecule from an alcohol to form an alkene

explanation:
Reduction involves gain of electrons, gain of hydrogen, or loss of oxygen. Ketones reduce to secondary alcohols; carboxylic acids reduce to primary alcohols.

Additional: hydrogen/loss of oxygen from a molecule
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What are common reducing agents used in drug synthesis?

options.a: Only water
options.b: NaBH4, LiAlH4
options.c: Only acids
options.d: Only bases

explanation:
Common reducing agents: NaBH4 (mild, reduces aldehydes/ketones), LiAlH4 (strong, reduces esters/acids), H2/Pd (catalytic hydrogenation), Zn/HCl (Clemmensen reduction).

Note: catalytic hydrogenation (H2/Pd), Zn/HCl
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What are common oxidizing agents used in drug synthesis?

options.a: Only oxygen gas
options.b: KMnO4, CrO3
options.c: Only bases
options.d: Only reducing agents

explanation:
Common oxidizing agents: KMnO4 (strong oxidizer), CrO3/Jones (alcohol to acid), PCC (alcohol to aldehyde), mCPBA (epoxidation), H2O2 (green oxidant).

Note: Jones reagent, PCC, H2O2, mCPBA
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is an aromatic compound?

options.a: A compound with a pleasant smell
options.b: A cyclic planar compound with conjugated
options.c: Any cyclic compound
options.d: Any organic compound

explanation:
Aromatic compounds are cyclic, planar, fully conjugated systems with 4n+2 pi electrons (Hückel's rule). Benzene (6 pi electrons, n=1) is the simplest example.

Note: 4n+2 pi electrons

Additional: pi electrons following Hückel's rule
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS)?

options.a: An electrophile replacing a hydrogen on an aromatic ring
options.b: A nucleophile replacing a hydrogen on an aromatic ring
options.c: An addition reaction on aromatic ring
options.d: A reduction of aromatic ring

explanation: EAS involves an electrophile (E+) attacking the electron-rich aromatic ring, substituting a hydrogen. Common types: nitration, halogenation, Friedel-Crafts reactions.
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Friedel-Crafts reaction?

options.a: A reaction between an alcohol and an acid
options.b: An electrophilic aromatic substitution using a Lewis acid
options.c: A reduction reaction
options.d: A hydrolysis reaction

explanation:
Friedel-Crafts: Alkylation (adds R group using RCl/AlCl3) or Acylation (adds RCO group using RCOCl/AlCl3). Important for synthesizing drug intermediates.

Additional: catalyst to introduce alkyl or acyl groups
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of nitro group reduction in drug synthesis?

options.a: Reduction of the nitro group has no practical value in synthesis
options.b: Nitro groups can be reduced to amino groups
options.c: Reducing a nitro group always increases the toxicity of the compound
options.d: Reducing a nitro group always makes the compound less water-soluble

explanation:
Reduction of -NO2 to -NH2 (using Sn/HCl, Fe/HCl, or catalytic hydrogenation) is crucial because the resulting amino group can be further modified (acylation, diazotization) to create many drugs.

Note: -NO2; -NH2

Additional: which are key intermediates for many drug molecules
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is diazotization?

options.a: Passing nitrogen gas through a cooled solution of an aromatic amine
options.b: Conversion of a primary aromatic amine to a diazonium salt using nitrous acid at 0-5 deg C
options.c: Treating an aromatic amine with sodium metal dissolved in liquid ammonia
options.d: Reducing an aromatic nitro compound to the corresponding primary amine

explanation:
Diazotization converts Ar-NH2 to Ar-N2+Cl- using NaNO2/HCl at 0-5°C. Diazonium salts are versatile intermediates for azo dyes, phenols, and various drug syntheses.

Additional: acid at 0-5°C to form a diazonium salt
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Baeyer-Villiger oxidation?

options.a: Addition of two hydrogen atoms across a carbon-carbon double bond
options.b: Insertion of an oxygen atom next to a carbonyl group
options.c: Decarboxylation of beta-keto acids to give smaller ketone molecules
options.d: Condensation of an aldehyde with an active methylene compound

explanation:
Baeyer-Villiger oxidation converts ketones to esters (or cyclic ketones to lactones) using peracids (mCPBA, peracetic acid). Important in steroid and lactone drug synthesis.

Note: ketone to ester or lactone

Additional: a carbonyl group using a peracid
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a heterocyclic compound?

options.a: A cyclic compound in which every ring atom is a carbon atom
options.b: A cyclic compound where the ring contains at least one atom other than carbon
options.c: An open-chain compound that contains no ring system at all
options.d: A compound that contains only one ring in its entire structure

explanation:
Heterocyclic compounds have rings containing heteroatoms (N, O, S). Examples: pyridine (N), furan (O), thiophene (S), pyrimidine (2N). Most drugs contain heterocyclic rings.

Note: N, O, S
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: Name common nitrogen-containing heterocyclic rings in drugs.

options.a: Only benzene rings
options.b: Pyridine, pyrimidine
options.c: Only six-membered rings
options.d: Only five-membered rings

explanation:
Key heterocyclic rings: Pyridine (isoniazid), Pyrimidine (sulfonamides), Indole (serotonin), Quinoline (quinine), Imidazole (antifungals), Morphine (piperidine+others).

Note: pyrrole, indole, quinoline, imidazole, piperidine, morpholine
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Beilstein test?

options.a: A test used to detect nitrogen in amino acids and amides
options.b: A test for detection of halogens in organic compounds
options.c: A test used to detect oxygen in alcohols and ethers
options.d: A test used to detect sulfur in thiols and thioethers

explanation:
The Beilstein test detects halogens (Cl, Br, I) in organic compounds. A copper wire coated with the compound is heated in a flame; a green/blue-green flame indicates halogens.

Additional: using a copper wire producing a green flame
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Lassaigne test used for?

options.a: Testing for metals
options.b: Detection of elements (N, S
options.c: Testing for pH
options.d: Testing for molecular weight

explanation:
Lassaigne test: the organic compound is fused with sodium to convert covalently bonded elements (N, S, halogens) into ionic forms that can be detected by simple qualitative tests.

Note: halogens) in organic compounds by fusing with sodium metal
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a carbonyl group?

options.a: -OH group of an alcohol
options.b: C=O group found in aldehydes, ketones
options.c: -NH2 group of an amine
options.d: -COOH group of a carboxylic acid

explanation:
The carbonyl group (C=O) is a polar functional group found in aldehydes (R-CHO), ketones (R-CO-R'), carboxylic acids (R-COOH), esters (R-COOR), and amides (R-CONH2).

Note: carboxylic acids, esters, and amides
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Schiff test used for?

options.a: Testing for the presence of hydroxyl groups in alcohols and phenols
options.b: Detection of aldehydes using Schiff's reagent, which turns magenta or pink
options.c: Testing for the presence of keto groups in simple ketones
options.d: Testing for free carboxylic acid groups in organic compounds

explanation:
Schiff reagent (magenta solution decolorized by SO2) turns pink/magenta in the presence of aldehydes. Ketones do not react. This differentiates aldehydes from ketones.

Note: fuchsin-sulfurous acid

Additional: reagent which turns magenta/pink
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is Tollens' test?

options.a: A test for the presence of alcohols in an aqueous solution
options.b: Detection of aldehydes using Tollens' reagent
options.c: A test for the presence of ketones in an aqueous solution
options.d: A test for the presence of amines in an aqueous solution

explanation:
Tollens' reagent [Ag(NH3)2]+ oxidizes aldehydes to carboxylic acids, and Ag+ is reduced to metallic silver forming a mirror on the tube wall. Ketones do not react.

Note: ammoniacal silver nitrate

Additional: — aldehydes produce a silver mirror
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of sulfonamide drugs?

options.a: They were the first antibacterial agents
options.b: They inhibit folic acid synthesis by competing with PABA
options.c: They are antifungal agents
options.d: They are antiviral agents

explanation: Sulfonamides (sulfa drugs) were the first antibacterial agents (Prontosil, 1935). They competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthase, blocking folic acid synthesis in bacteria.
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the structure-activity relationship of sulfonamides?

options.a: Any modification to any part of the molecule is equally well tolerated
options.b: The para-amino group must be free for antibacterial activity
options.c: The substituent at the para position has no influence on activity
options.d: Only the sulfur atom of the sulfonamide group determines the activity

explanation:
SAR of sulfonamides: 1) Free -NH2 at para position essential. 2) SO2NH- must be present. 3) R group on N1 affects potency, spectrum, and pharmacokinetics.

Note: not acylated

Additional: on the sulfonamide nitrogen modify potency and spectrum

Note: substitutions
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the general structure of a barbiturate?

options.a: A five-membered ring
options.b: Barbituric acid — pyrimidine-trione ring
options.c: A benzene ring
options.d: A six-membered nitrogen ring

explanation:
Barbiturates are derivatives of barbituric acid (2,4,6-trioxohexahydropyrimidine). Substitutions at C5 position determine the duration of action and potency.

Note: malonylurea

Additional: with substituents at C5
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: How do barbiturates act as sedatives?

options.a: By blocking GABA receptors and reducing chloride influx into neurons
options.b: By enhancing GABAergic inhibition — they increase chloride channel opening
options.c: By inhibiting the reuptake of noradrenaline from the synaptic cleft
options.d: By activating dopamine D2 receptors in the limbic system of the brain

explanation:
Barbiturates bind to an allosteric site on GABA-A receptors, increasing the duration of chloride ion channel opening, enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission in the CNS.

Additional: duration of chloride channel opening at GABA-A receptors
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the general structure of a benzodiazepine?

options.a: Fused benzene and pyrimidine rings
options.b: Fused benzene and diazepine rings
options.c: Fused benzene and pyrrole rings
options.d: A single benzene ring

explanation:
Benzodiazepines have a benzene ring fused to a 7-membered diazepine ring containing 2 nitrogen atoms. Key substituents at positions 1, 5, and 7 determine activity.

Note: 7-membered ring with 2 N
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: How do benzodiazepines differ from barbiturates in mechanism?

options.a: Same mechanism
options.b: Benzodiazepines increase FREQUENCY of chloride
options.c: Benzodiazepines block GABA
options.d: Barbiturates block chloride channels

explanation:
Both enhance GABA-A activity: benzodiazepines increase the frequency of chloride channel opening (partial agonist), while barbiturates increase the duration (more potent, more dangerous).

Additional: channel opening; barbiturates increase DURATION
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the general structure of a sulfonamide antibiotic?

options.a: R-SO2-NH-R' with sulfur in the ring structure
options.b: Para-aminobenzene sulfonamide with various R
options.c: R-COOH with a free carboxylic acid group
options.d: R-NH2 only without any sulfonyl group present

explanation:
Sulfonamide antibiotics have the structure: p-NH2-C6H4-SO2-NH-R. The para-amino group is essential. R substituents modify the spectrum, potency, and pharmacokinetics.

Additional: substituents on the sulfonamide nitrogen
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is paracetamol (acetaminophen) synthesized from?

options.a: Salicylic acid
options.b: p-Aminophenol by acetylation
options.c: Benzoic acid
options.d: Phenol and acetic acid

explanation:
Paracetamol is synthesized by acetylation of p-aminophenol with acetic anhydride (or acetyl chloride). p-Aminophenol itself can be made by reduction of p-nitrophenol.

Additional: with acetic anhydride
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What are the metabolites of paracetamol?

options.a: Only inactive glucuronide conjugates formed in the liver
options.b: Glucuronide and sulfate conjugates, and NAPQI
options.c: Only the toxic metabolite NAPQI, which is always formed
options.d: Metabolites identical to those produced from aspirin

explanation:
Paracetamol is metabolized by: 1) Glucuronidation (55%) → non-toxic. 2) Sulfation (35%) → non-toxic. 3) CYP2E1 oxidation (5-10%) → NAPQI (toxic), detoxified by glutathione. Overdose depletes glutathione → hepatotoxicity.

Note: toxic reactive metabolite via CYP2E1
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is NAPQI?

options.a: A brand name of paracetamol tablets
options.b: N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine — a toxic reactive
options.c: A type of over-the-counter painkiller
options.d: An excipient used in tablet manufacturing

explanation:
NAPQI is the toxic metabolite of paracetamol formed by cytochrome P450 (CYP2E1). Normally detoxified by glutathione conjugation. In overdose, glutathione is depleted → NAPQI causes liver cell death.

Additional: metabolite of paracetamol formed by CYP2E1
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the antidote for paracetamol poisoning?

options.a: Sodium bicarbonate given intravenously to alkalinize the urine
options.b: N-acetylcysteine — replenishes glutathione
options.c: Vitamin K to correct the bleeding tendency that develops in overdose
options.d: Broad-spectrum antibiotics to prevent secondary bacterial infection

explanation:
N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is the antidote for paracetamol overdose. It replenishes glutathione (GSH) stores and provides sulfhydryl groups for NAPQI detoxification, preventing liver damage.

Additional: stores to detoxify NAPQI
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the general structure of a quinolone antibiotic?

options.a: A large lactone ring containing many carbon atoms, like the macrolides
options.b: A 4-quinolone nucleus with substituents
options.c: A linear system of four fused six-membered rings, like the tetracyclines
options.d: A five-membered ring containing a sulfur atom, like the penicillins

explanation:
Quinolones have a 4-oxo-1,4-dihydroquinoline nucleus. Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin) have fluorine at C-6 for enhanced activity. Substituents at various positions modify activity and spectrum.

Note: 6, 7, and 8

Note: or 4-fluoroquinolone

Additional: at positions 1 3
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the mechanism of action of fluoroquinolones?

options.a: Inhibiting cell wall synthesis
options.b: Inhibiting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
options.c: Inhibiting protein synthesis
options.d: Inhibiting folic acid synthesis

explanation:
Fluoroquinolones bind to and inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, preventing DNA supercoiling and causing double-strand breaks, leading to bacterial cell death.

Note: topoisomerase II

Additional: preventing DNA replication and transcription
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the general structure of a cephalosporin?

options.a: A benzene ring
options.b: A beta-lactam ring fused
options.c: A five-membered ring
options.d: A pyrimidine ring

explanation:
Cephalosporins have a beta-lactam ring fused to a 6-membered dihydrothiazine ring (vs penicillin's 5-membered thiazolidine ring). This makes them more resistant to beta-lactamase.

Note: 6-membered sulfur-containing ring

Additional: to a dihydrothiazine ring
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the difference between penicillins and cephalosporins structurally?

options.a: No difference
options.b: Penicillin:
options.c: Penicillin has no beta-lactam
options.d: Cephalosporins are not beta-lactams

explanation:
Both are beta-lactam antibiotics. Penicillins have a 5-membered thiazolidine ring fused to beta-lactam. Cephalosporins have a 6-membered dihydrothiazine ring, making them more stable to beta-lactamases.

Note: beta-lactam + 5-membered thiazolidine ring; Cephalosporin: beta-lactam + 6-membered dihydrothiazine ring
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the role of the beta-lactam ring in penicillin activity?

options.a: It only improves the stability of the drug during oral administration
options.b: It is the pharmacophore - it mimics the natural substrate and binds penicillin-binding proteins, blocking cell wall synthesis
options.c: It helps the drug dissolve rapidly in the acidic contents of the stomach
options.d: It is converted in the liver into an active metabolite that kills bacteria

explanation:
The beta-lactam ring is the essential pharmacophore. It mimics the D-Ala-D-Ala substrate of transpeptidase (PBP), binding irreversibly and inhibiting cell wall cross-linking.

Note: PBPs

Additional: binds to penicillin-binding proteins inhibiting cell wall synthesis
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of the 6-aminopenicillanic acid (6-APA) nucleus?

options.a: It is a metabolic breakdown product of penicillin that is excreted unchanged
options.b: It is the core structure from which all semi-synthetic penicillins are derived by modifying the side chain
options.c: It is a compound that blocks the antibacterial action of all penicillins
options.d: It is a toxic impurity formed during the fermentation of penicillin

explanation:
6-APA is obtained from natural penicillin by removing the side chain. It serves as the starting material for synthesizing semi-synthetic penicillins with improved properties.

Additional: penicillins are derived by modifying the side chain
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Claisen condensation?

options.a: An addition reaction between two molecules of an unsaturated hydrocarbon
options.b: A carbon-carbon bond-forming reaction between two esters or carbonyl compounds
options.c: A condensation of an aldehyde with an aromatic amine to form a Schiff base
options.d: A rearrangement of an ester into a ketone under strongly acidic conditions

explanation:
Claisen condensation involves base-catalyzed condensation of two ester molecules to form a beta-keto ester. It is an important C-C bond-forming reaction in drug synthesis.

Note: or an ester and a ketone

Additional: esters using a strong base
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Knoevenagel condensation?

options.a: A condensation between an aldehyde/ketone and an active methylene compound
options.b: A condensation between an aldehyde and an amine to form a Schiff base
options.c: An oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carbonyl compound using a mild oxidant
options.d: A hydrolysis of an ester into an acid and an alcohol using dilute alkali

explanation:
Knoevenagel condensation involves reaction of an aldehyde or ketone with an active methylene compound (malonic acid, acetoacetic ester) using a mild base catalyst.

Additional: active methylene compound using a weak base
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Grignard reaction?

options.a: A hydrolysis reaction in which an ester is split by water into an acid and an alcohol
options.b: An organometallic reaction where RMgX reacts
options.c: An oxidation reaction converting a primary alcohol into a carboxylic acid
options.d: A substitution reaction replacing a hydroxyl group with a chlorine atom

explanation:
Grignard reaction uses R-Mg-X (alkyl/aryl magnesium halide) as a nucleophile attacking carbonyl carbons. Formaldehyde gives primary alcohol; other aldehydes give secondary; ketones give tertiary.

Note: Grignard reagent

Additional: with carbonyl compounds to form alcohols
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is hydrogen bonding and its significance in drug-receptor interaction?

options.a: A strong covalent force that holds the two hydrogen atoms of an H2 molecule together
options.b: A weak attraction between a hydrogen atom and an electronegative atom such as N, O or F, important in drug-receptor binding
options.c: An ionic attraction between a hydrogen ion and a chloride ion dissolved in solution
options.d: A repulsive force that acts between the nonpolar hydrocarbon chains of lipids

explanation:
Hydrogen bonds (O-H...O, N-H...O) are weaker than covalent bonds but collectively very important for drug-receptor interactions, protein folding, and DNA base pairing.

Additional: atom and another electronegative atom — crucial for drug-receptor binding
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of lipophilicity in drug design?

options.a: Lipophilic drugs are always better
options.b: Lipophilicity affects absorption, distribution
options.c: Lipophilicity has no importance
options.d: Only hydrophilic drugs work

explanation:
Lipophilicity (measured by logP) is crucial: moderate lipophilicity is needed for membrane absorption, but too high causes poor solubility. It affects distribution, protein binding, and metabolism.

Note: metabolism, and membrane permeability — measured by logP
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is logP in medicinal chemistry?

options.a: The logarithm of the acid dissociation constant of a drug in aqueous solution
options.b: The logarithm of the partition coefficient between octanol and water
options.c: A measure of the drug's ability to form hydrogen bonds with water molecules
options.d: The ratio of ionized to unionized drug at the pH of the stomach

explanation:
logP = log([drug]octanol/[drug]water). High logP = lipophilic; low logP = hydrophilic. Optimal logP for oral drugs is typically 1-3 for good absorption.

Note: octanol/water

Additional: a measure of a drug's lipophilicity
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the importance of pKa in drug design?

options.a: pKa has no effect on how a drug behaves once it enters the body
options.b: pKa determines the ionization state of a drug at a given pH
options.c: pKa determines the molecular weight of the drug and its melting point
options.d: pKa measures the analgesic potency of a drug at its site of action

explanation:
pKa determines what fraction of drug is ionized vs unionized at physiological pH (7.4). Unionized forms cross membranes more easily (absorption); ionized forms are more soluble.

Note: distribution, and binding

Additional: drug at physiological pH affecting absorption
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is Lipinski's Rule of Five?

options.a: A set of guidelines for predicting a drug's melting point from its chemical structure
options.b: Guidelines predicting drug-likeness and oral bioavailability
options.c: A rule stating that all approved drugs must have a molecular weight below 100 daltons
options.d: A guideline for choosing the correct dosage form for a newly discovered drug

explanation:
Lipinski's Rule of Five predicts good oral bioavailability: MW ≤500 Da, logP ≤5, ≤5 H-bond donors (NH, OH), ≤10 H-bond acceptors (N, O). Violation of >1 rule suggests poor absorption.

Note: H-bond donors <5, H-bond acceptors <10

Note: MW <500, logP <5
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a Michael acceptor in drug chemistry?

options.a: A type of receptor on cell membranes
options.b: An alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl compound that accepts electrons
options.c: An enzyme inhibitor of cytochrome P450
options.d: A drug metabolite formed in the liver

explanation:
Michael acceptors (e.g., acrylamides, vinyl ketones) have an electrophilic double bond conjugated with a carbonyl. They react with nucleophiles (thiols, amines) via Michael addition.

Additional: undergoes Michael addition with nucleophiles
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Robinson annulation?

options.a: A pericyclic reaction forming a six-membered ring from a conjugated diene
options.b: A ring-forming reaction combining Michael addition with aldol condensation
options.c: An acid-catalyzed dehydration of a cyclic alcohol to a cycloalkene
options.d: A rearrangement of an alpha-hydroxy ketone into a diketone

explanation:
Robinson annulation combines Michael addition of a ketone to a vinyl ketone followed by intramolecular aldol condensation, forming a new six-membered ring. Important in steroid synthesis.

Additional: intramolecular aldol condensation to form a six-membered ring
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is diazepam's chemical classification?

options.a: Barbiturate with marked sedative action
options.b: Benzodiazepine — 1 4-benzodiazepine with a chlorophenyl group
options.c: Phenothiazine with antipsychotic action profile
options.d: Imidazopyridine with hypnotic action profile

explanation:
Diazepam is a 1,4-benzodiazepine with Cl at position 7, phenyl at C5, and methyl on N1. It enhances GABAergic inhibition in the CNS.

Additional: at C5 and a methyl group on N1
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the general structure of a sulfonamide drug?

options.a: An aliphatic sulfonamide that contains no aromatic ring in the molecule
options.b: Parasubstituted benzene sulfonamide with a free para-amino group
options.c: A sulfonamide in which the para-amino group is acetylated before use
options.d: A para-hydroxy benzoic acid ester carrying an aromatic amine side chain

explanation:
Sulfonamide drugs share the structure p-NH2-C6H4-SO2-NH-R. The free para-amino group and sulfonamide group are essential for antibacterial activity.

Note: 4-NH2-C6H4-SO2-NH-R
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is ibuprofen's chemical classification?

options.a: Paracetamol derivative
options.b: Propionic acid derivative
options.c: Salicylate
options.d: Acetic acid derivative

explanation:
Ibuprofen is a propionic acid derivative NSAID (2-(4-isobutylphenyl)propionic acid). It inhibits COX-1 and COX-2, reducing prostaglandin synthesis.

Note: 2-arylpropionic acid NSAID
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the mechanism of action of aspirin?

options.a: Inhibiting COX enzymes irreversibly by acetylating a serine residue in the active site
options.b: Inhibiting COX enzymes reversibly by competing with arachidonic acid at the active site
options.c: Blocking histamine H1 receptors that mediate pain and inflammation
options.d: Blocking dopamine receptors in the central nervous system

explanation:
Aspirin irreversibly acetylates Ser530 of COX-1 (and COX-2), blocking the active site and preventing conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandin H2. This inhibits thromboxane A2 in platelets.

Additional: serine residue preventing prostaglandin synthesis
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the difference between COX-1 and COX-2?

options.a: No difference
options.b: COX-1 is constitutive; COX-2 is inducible
options.c: COX-2 is always present
options.d: COX-1 causes inflammation only

explanation:
COX-1 is constitutively expressed (gastric mucosa protection, platelet aggregation, renal function). COX-2 is induced at sites of inflammation (produces prostaglandins causing pain, fever, swelling).

Note: inflammatory, pain, fever

Note: protective, platelet function
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the structural difference between aspirin and salicylic acid?

options.a: Both molecules have identical substituents on the aromatic ring
options.b: Aspirin has an acetyl group replacing the -OH of salicylic acid
options.c: Aspirin has no carboxyl group while salicylic acid has two of them
options.d: Salicylic acid carries an acetyl group while aspirin carries a hydroxyl group

explanation: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) = salicylic acid with the phenolic -OH acetylated (-OCOCH3). Salicylic acid has a free -OH group which is more irritating to the stomach.
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the chemical name of caffeine?

options.a: 1,3,7-Trimethylxanthine
options.b: 3,7-Dimethylxanthine
options.c: 1,3-Dimethyluric acid
options.d: 1,7-Dimethylxanthine

explanation: Caffeine is 1,3,7-trimethylxanthine (a trimethylated xanthine alkaloid). It is a methylxanthine like theophylline (1,3-dimethylxanthine) and theobromine (3,7-dimethylxanthine).
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the structural relationship between caffeine, theophylline, and theobromine?

options.a: They are stereoisomers of one another with identical pharmacological effects
options.b: All are methylxanthines differing in the number and position of methyl groups
options.c: They all contain a purine ring carrying three acetyl groups in different positions
options.d: They differ from one another only in the length of their carbon side chains

explanation:
All three are methylxanthines. Caffeine: 1,3,7-trimethyl. Theophylline: 1,3-dimethyl (bronchodilator). Theobromine: 3,7-dimethyl (cocoa). Small structural differences → different pharmacological profiles.

Additional: position of methyl groups on the xanthine ring
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of methylation of the xanthine ring?

options.a: No significance
options.b: Methylation increases CNS stimulant
options.c: Methylation decreases all activity
options.d: Methylation makes the drug toxic

explanation:
Methylation of xanthine increases CNS stimulation (caffeine > theophylline > theobromine) and reduces diuretic activity. Trimethylation (caffeine) gives strongest CNS effect.

Note: and improves oral bioavailability

Additional: activity decreases diuretic effect
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the synthesis of paracetamol from phenol?

options.a: Direct acetylation of the phenolic hydroxyl group with acetic anhydride
options.b: Nitration of phenol, then reduction and acetylation
options.c: Oxidation of phenol to benzoquinone followed by reaction with ammonia
options.d: Chlorination of phenol followed by replacement of chlorine with an amine

explanation:
Industrial synthesis: Phenol → nitration (HNO3) → p-nitrophenol → reduction (Sn/HCl or catalytic hydrogenation) → p-aminophenol → acetylation (acetic anhydride) → paracetamol.

Additional: p-aminophenol → acetylation with acetic anhydride
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the condensation reaction between an amine and a carboxylic acid?

options.a: Esterification of an alcohol and acid
options.b: Amide bond formation with loss of water
options.c: Aldol condensation of two aldehydes
options.d: Michael addition to an alkene

explanation:
Reaction of -NH2 (amine) with -COOH (carboxylic acid) forms an amide bond (-CONH-) with loss of water. This is the basis of peptide and protein formation.

Note: peptide bond formation

Additional: release of water
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Grignard reagent?

options.a: An acid with a carboxyl functional group
options.b: An organomagnesium compound used as a carbon nucleophile
options.c: A base with a hydroxyl functional group
options.d: A catalyst used for esterification reactions

explanation:
Grignard reagents (R-Mg-X) are formed by reacting alkyl/aryl halides with magnesium metal in dry ether. They are powerful nucleophiles that attack carbonyl carbons.

Note: RMgX

Additional: strong nucleophile in organic synthesis
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Cannizzaro reaction?

options.a: Reaction of aldehydes with no alpha-hydrogens in concentrated alkali
options.b: Oxidation of secondary alcohols to ketones using a strong oxidizing agent
options.c: Condensation of two aldehydes that have alpha-hydrogens, in dilute alkali
options.d: Reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride

explanation:
Cannizzaro reaction: aldehydes without alpha-H (e.g., formaldehyde, benzaldehyde) undergo base-catalyzed disproportionation to give a primary alcohol and a carboxylic acid salt.

Additional: strong base to give alcohol and carboxylic acid salt
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the purpose of drug chirality in pharmaceutical chemistry?

options.a: It has no purpose
options.b: Enantiomers may have different
options.c: Chiral drugs are cheaper
options.d: Chiral drugs are always racemic

explanation:
Different enantiomers can have different activities: S-ibuprofen (active), R-naproxen (toxic), S-omeprazole (more potent). Single enantiomer drugs (chiral switches) can improve safety and efficacy.

Note: and pharmacokinetics — single enantiomers can be safer and more effective

Additional: pharmacological activities toxicities
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a pharmacological antagonist?

options.a: A drug that activates the receptor and produces the same effect as the natural agonist
options.b: A drug that binds to a receptor without activating it, blocking the agonist
options.c: A drug that increases the synthesis of the natural agonist inside the body
options.d: A substance that permanently destroys the receptor protein at the cell surface

explanation:
A pharmacological antagonist binds to a receptor and prevents the agonist from binding or activating it. Example: propranolol (beta-blocker) antagonizes norepinephrine at beta receptors.

Additional: activating it blocking the action of an agonist
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the difference between competitive and non-competitive antagonism?

options.a: The two mechanisms of antagonism are identical in every respect
options.b: Competitive antagonist competes with agonist for the same receptor site
options.c: Competitive antagonism is always the clinically preferred mechanism
options.d: Non-competitive antagonism is always weaker than the competitive type

explanation:
Competitive antagonists bind to the same site as the agonist and can be overcome by increasing agonist concentration (rightward shift of dose-response curve). Non-competitive antagonists bind irreversibly or allosterically.

Note: insurmountable

Additional: same binding site; non-competitive binds elsewhere
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Hammett equation in drug design?

options.a: A rule relating a drug's partition coefficient to its lipid solubility
options.b: A mathematical relationship between reaction rates and substituent effects
options.c: A formula for calculating the maintenance dose from body surface area
options.d: An equation linking a reaction rate to the concentration of its catalyst

explanation:
Hammett equation: log(k/k0) = σρ. It quantifies how electron-withdrawing or electron-donating substituents on aromatic rings affect reaction rates and drug activity.

Additional: electronic effects of substituents on benzene rings
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a bioisostere?

options.a: A biological organism used in drug testing
options.b: An atom or group that can replace another while keeping similar biological activity
options.c: A toxic metabolite formed during drug metabolism
options.d: A drug excipient added for tablet binding

explanation:
Bioisosteres are substituents with similar physicochemical properties: -F for -H (similar size, different electronics), -COOH for tetrazole (same pKa), -CH3 for -Cl (similar volume).

Note: or electronic properties

Additional: maintaining similar biological activity due to similar size shape
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: Give examples of classical bioisosteres.

options.a: -CH3 and -OH
options.b: -F/-H, -COOH/-SO3H/-PO3H2
options.c: -Cl and -Br only
options.d: All atoms are bioisosteres

explanation:
Classical bioisosteres: Halogen for H, carboxylic acid for tetrazole/sulfonic acid, hydroxyl for amine, benzene for pyridine/furan. These replace groups while maintaining activity.

Note: -NH2/-OH, benzene/pyridine rings
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of the Michaelis-Menten equation in pharmacology?

options.a: It calculates the volume of distribution of a drug from its dose and plasma level
options.b: It describes enzyme kinetics relating reaction velocity to substrate concentration
options.c: It predicts the therapeutic index of a drug from its lethal and effective doses
options.d: It describes the rate at which a drug is filtered by the glomerulus of the kidney

explanation:
Michaelis-Menten: V = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]). Vmax is maximum velocity; Km is substrate concentration at half Vmax (measure of enzyme-substrate affinity).

Note: V = Vmax[S]/, relating reaction velocity to substrate concentration
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the difference between Km and Vmax?

options.a: Km is the maximum velocity while Vmax is the substrate concentration at half that velocity
options.b: Km is substrate concentration at half-Vmax; Vmax is the maximum reaction rate
options.c: Km is measured in moles of product formed per minute per milligram of enzyme
options.d: Vmax is the substrate concentration at which the enzyme reaches half its maximum velocity

explanation:
Km reflects enzyme-substrate affinity (lower Km = higher affinity). Vmax is the maximum rate when enzyme is fully saturated with substrate. Both are important in drug-enzyme interactions.

Note: measure of affinity

Additional: Vmax is maximum reaction velocity
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a Lineweaver-Burk plot?

options.a: A plot of concentration vs time
options.b: A double reciprocal plot used to determine Km
options.c: A pH curve
options.d: A solubility curve

explanation:
Lineweaver-Burk: 1/V = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. The y-intercept gives 1/Vmax, x-intercept gives -1/Km. Different inhibitor types give distinct patterns on this plot.

Note: 1/V vs 1/[S]

Additional: and Vmax and identify type of enzyme inhibition
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is bioavailability?

options.a: The amount of drug that reaches systemic circulation unchanged
options.b: The total amount of drug that was administered to the patient
options.c: The fraction of the dose that is metabolized before reaching the blood
options.d: The fraction of the dose that is excreted unchanged by the kidneys

explanation:
Bioavailability (F) = fraction of drug reaching systemic circulation in unchanged form. IV = 100% bioavailability. Oral <100% due to first-pass metabolism and incomplete absorption.

Additional: expressed as a percentage of the administered dose
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the first-pass effect?

options.a: Rapid excretion of a drug by the kidney immediately after intravenous injection
options.b: Metabolism of a drug in the gut wall and liver before systemic circulation
options.c: Binding of a drug to plasma albumin shortly after oral administration
options.d: The initial distribution of a drug into adipose tissue after absorption

explanation:
First-pass metabolism: oral drugs absorbed from GI tract go via portal vein to liver where they may be extensively metabolized before reaching systemic circulation. E.g., morphine (70% first-pass).

Additional: liver before reaching systemic circulation reducing oral bioavailability
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the biological source of digitalis?

options.a: Thevetia peruviana leaves
options.b: Dried leaves of Digitalis purpurea
options.c: Strophanthus kombe seeds
options.d: Nerium oleander leaves

explanation:
Digitalis is from Digitalis purpurea Linn. (family Plantaginaceae). D. lanata is the source of digoxin. Both contain cardiac glycosides.

Note: foxglove
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the difference between inhibitory constant (Ki) and IC50?

options.a: Ki is the inhibitor concentration that produces 50% inhibition of the enzyme
options.b: Ki is the dissociation constant of inhibitor from the enzyme
options.c: Ki is measured only in living animals while IC50 is always measured in the test tube
options.d: IC50 is the dissociation constant of the inhibitor-enzyme complex

explanation:
Ki is an intrinsic binding constant (independent of assay conditions). IC50 is the concentration causing 50% inhibition, which depends on substrate concentration and assay conditions.

Note: depends on assay conditions

Additional: enzyme; IC50 is concentration causing 50% inhibition
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a Michaelis-Menten inhibitor?

options.a: An inhibitor that was first discovered by a scientist named Michaelis
options.b: An inhibitor that increases Km without changing Vmax
options.c: A substance that binds to the substrate rather than to the enzyme itself
options.d: An enzyme activator that lowers the value of Km for the reaction

explanation:
Michaelis-Menten inhibition describes how competitive, non-competitive, and uncompetitive inhibitors affect enzyme kinetics differently, changing Km, Vmax, or both.

Additional: characteristic changes in Km and/or Vmax
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is an uncompetitive inhibitor?

options.a: An inhibitor that binds to the free enzyme
options.b: An inhibitor that binds only to the enzyme-substrate complex
options.c: An inhibitor that binds irreversibly
options.d: An inhibitor that activates the enzyme

explanation:
Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only to the ES complex (not free enzyme). Both Km and Vmax decrease by the same factor, so the Lineweaver-Burk plot shows parallel lines.

Additional: enzyme-substrate complex decreasing both Km and Vmax
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation?

options.a: pH = pKa + log([acid]/[base]), used to find the acidity of pure water
options.b: pH = pKa + log [A-]/[HA] — used to find drug ionization
options.c: pH = pKa - log([A-]/[HA]), which gives the pKa when pH equals zero
options.d: pH = pKa x ([A-]/[HA]), relating pH directly to the buffer concentration

explanation:
Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) for weak acids. For weak bases: pH = pKa + log([B]/[BH+]). Critical for predicting drug ionization at physiological pH.

Note: [base]/[acid]

Additional: calculate pH of buffer solutions and drug ionization
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of drug ionization for absorption?

options.a: Ionized drugs are always absorbed more rapidly across lipid membranes
options.b: Unionized drugs cross lipid membranes more easily; ionized drugs do not
options.c: The state of ionization has no effect on drug absorption at any site
options.d: Only completely neutral drug molecules can ever be absorbed from the gut

explanation:
The pH-partition hypothesis: unionized forms cross membranes better. Weak acids are better absorbed in stomach (acidic pH, more unionized). Weak bases in intestine (alkaline pH).

Note: non-ionized

Additional: water-soluble and better absorbed in ionized form from some sites

Note: ionized forms are more
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the drug's partition coefficient?

options.a: The amount of drug that dissolves in water at a given temperature
options.b: The ratio of drug concentration in oil and water phases
options.c: The ratio of ionized to unionized drug at the pH of the stomach
options.d: The extent to which a drug binds to plasma proteins after absorption

explanation:
The partition coefficient (P or logP) = [drug]organic/[drug]aqueous. It measures the drug's lipophilicity, which affects absorption, distribution, protein binding, and membrane permeability.

Note: typically octanol and water

Additional: two immiscible phases — measures lipophilicity
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is crystal polymorphism in pharmaceutical chemistry?

options.a: Contamination of drug crystals by microorganisms during storage
options.b: The ability of a drug to exist in multiple crystalline forms
options.c: The breakdown of a drug crystal into its amorphous form on heating
options.d: The ability of different drugs to co-crystallize together in one lattice

explanation:
Polymorphism: same drug molecule can crystallize in different forms (polymorphs) with different melting points, solubility, stability, and bioavailability. Ritonavir case: Form II was less soluble, causing product failure.

Additional: different crystalline forms with different physical properties
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of salt selection in drug formulation?

options.a: It has no significance
options.b: Different salt forms of the same active ingredient
options.c: Only one salt form exists
options.d: Salt forms don't affect absorption

explanation:
