Salt selection affects: solubility (determines dissolution rate), stability, hygroscopicity, processing properties, and bioavailability. E.g., metformin HCl vs metformin hydrochloride.

Note: stability, and bioavailability

Additional: drug have different solubility dissolution rate
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a soft drug?

options.a: A drug that is very easily absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract
options.b: A drug designed to be metabolized to an inactive form
options.c: A drug that dissolves quickly on the tongue without any water
options.d: A drug that produces only very gentle pharmacological effects

explanation:
Soft drugs (e.g., esmolol, loteprednol) are designed to have predictable, rapid metabolism to inactive metabolites after their site of action, reducing systemic side effects.

Additional: after exerting its therapeutic effect limiting duration of action
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is a hard drug?

options.a: A drug that is difficult to administer
options.b: A drug that is not metabolized or minimally metabolized
options.c: A solid drug
options.d: A strong drug

explanation:
Hard drugs resist metabolic degradation (e.g., cyclosporine, diazepam). They remain active for longer but may accumulate and cause more side effects compared to soft drugs.

Additional: maintaining activity throughout its residence in the body
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of the amide bond in peptides and proteins?

options.a: The amide bond has no effect on the shape or stability of proteins
options.b: It provides structural rigidity, stability to hydrolysis
options.c: The amide bond is freely rotating and very easily hydrolyzed in water
options.d: The amide bond is found only in nucleic acids and never in proteins

explanation:
The amide (peptide) bond has partial double bond character due to resonance, making it planar and rigid. This constrains protein folding. It is stable to hydrolysis under physiological conditions.

Note: and serves as the backbone linking amino acids
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Bischler-Napieralski reaction?

options.a: A condensation reaction between two molecules of a simple ester
options.b: A cyclization of beta-phenylethylamides using P2O5 or POCl3
options.c: An oxidation reaction converting a primary alcohol into an aldehyde
options.d: A reduction reaction converting a nitro group into an amino group

explanation:
Bischler-Napieralski: cyclodehydration of N-acyl-beta-phenylethylamine using Lewis acid (P2O5, POCl3) to form 3,4-dihydroisoquinoline. Key step in synthesizing isoquinoline alkaloids.

Additional: to form dihydroisoquinolines — important in alkaloid synthesis
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Pictet-Spengler reaction?

options.a: A condensation of two molecules of a simple aliphatic ketone
options.b: A condensation of a beta-arylethylamine with an aldehyde
options.c: A dehydration reaction that forms an alkene from a primary alcohol
options.d: A nucleophilic substitution reaction on an aromatic ring by an amine

explanation:
Pictet-Spengler: beta-arylethylamine + aldehyde → Schiff base → acid-catalyzed ring closure → tetrahydroisoquinoline. Important in biosynthesis and synthesis of alkaloids.

Additional: aldehyde/ketone followed by cyclization to form tetrahydroisoquinolines
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Curtius rearrangement?

options.a: A rearrangement of alkenes to cyclopropanes
options.b: Thermal decomposition of an acyl azide to an isocyanate with loss of nitrogen
options.c: A condensation reaction of two aldehydes
options.d: A reduction reaction of a nitro group

explanation:
Curtius: RCON3 → R-N=C=O + N2. The isocyanate is hydrolyzed to amine. Used to convert carboxylic acids to amines with one fewer carbon atom.

Additional: loss of N2 used to convert carboxylic acids to amines
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Hofmann rearrangement?

options.a: A reaction in which primary alcohols are dehydrated to alkenes
options.b: Conversion of a primary amide to a primary amine with one fewer carbon atom, using bromine and alkali
options.c: An oxidation of primary amines to nitro compounds using strong oxidants
options.d: A condensation of two amide molecules with elimination of ammonia

explanation:
Hofmann: RCONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH → RNH2 + Na2CO3 + 2NaBr. Converts primary amide to amine with loss of carbonyl carbon (one fewer carbon).

Additional: amine with one fewer carbon using Br2/NaOH
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Gabriel phthalimide synthesis?

options.a: A method to synthesize carboxylic acids
options.b: A method to prepare pure primary amines from alkyl halides
options.c: A method to synthesize esters
options.d: A method to prepare alcohols

explanation:
Gabriel synthesis: phthalimide + KOH → potassium phthalimide, then + R-X → N-alkylphthalimide, then hydrazinolysis → pure primary amine (RNH2). Avoids over-alkylation problem.

Additional: alkyl halides via phthalimide intermediate avoiding polyalkylation
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of the phenol group in drug molecules?

options.a: It has no significance
options.b: Phenols can form hydrogen bonds
options.c: Phenols are always toxic
options.d: Phenols cannot participate in reactions

explanation:
Phenols are important: hydrogen bond donors/acceptors, can be oxidized, electron-rich aromatic ring participates in EAS, common pharmacophore in analgesics (salicylates), hormones (estradiol), and neurotransmitters.

Note: and are common in many drugs; salicylates, morphine, tyrosine

Note: undergo oxidation to quinones
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of the carboxylic acid group in drugs?

options.a: It serves only to make the drug acidic and has no other useful function
options.b: It enables salt formation for solubility, participates in hydrogen bonding
options.c: It is always removed from the molecule during first-pass metabolism
options.d: It prevents the drug from binding to plasma proteins in the blood

explanation:
Carboxylic acids: enable salt formation (improving solubility), act as hydrogen bond donors/acceptors, can be esterified for prodrugs, and are present in NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac).

Note: and can be modified to esters (prodrugs) or amides
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of the amino group in drug molecules?

options.a: It has no significance
options.b: Amino groups can be protonated
options.c: Amino groups make drugs inactive
options.d: Amino groups are toxic always

explanation:
Amino groups: protonate at physiological pH (forming water-soluble salts), hydrogen bond, participate in nucleophilic reactions, found in many drugs (sulfonamides, local anesthetics, antihistamines).

Note: and are common in many drugs

Note: forming salts for solubility

Note: participate in hydrogen bonding
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of the halogen atom in drug design?

options.a: Bromine substitution always reduces the lipophilicity of an aromatic drug
options.b: Fluorine enhances metabolic stability and lipophilicity, improving drug action
options.c: Iodine substitution has no effect at all on the metabolic half-life of a drug
options.d: Adding a halogen to a molecule always increases its water solubility

explanation:
Halogens in drug design: F (increases metabolic stability, bioisostere for H, improves membrane permeability), Cl/Br (increase lipophilicity, can form halogen bonds with proteins), I (used in radiocontrast).

Additional: increase lipophilicity and can participate in binding

Note: chlorine/bromine
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the difference between a drug's intrinsic activity and efficacy?

options.a: Intrinsic activity is the dose of a drug that produces half of the maximum response
options.b: Intrinsic activity is the ability to activate a receptor; efficacy is the resulting response
options.c: Efficacy refers to the affinity of the drug for its binding site on the receptor
options.d: Intrinsic activity describes the rate at which a drug is absorbed and distributed

explanation:
Intrinsic activity (a): ability of drug to activate receptor (full agonist a=1, partial agonist 0<a<1, antagonist a=0). Efficacy: maximum therapeutic effect achievable in a clinical setting.

Note: 0-1 scale

Additional: is the maximum response a drug can produce in vivo

Note: efficacy
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Clark's occupancy theory?

options.a: A theory describing how much space a drug occupies in the body after injection
options.b: A theory stating that drug response is proportional to receptor occupancy
options.c: A theory about how drugs should be stored to occupy less warehouse space
options.d: A theory of how cells rearrange themselves to occupy tissue in an organ

explanation:
Clark's theory: Drug response = proportion of receptors occupied. Occupancy depends on drug concentration and receptor affinity (Kd). Limitations: doesn't account for spare receptors or partial agonists.

Additional: the fraction of receptors occupied by the drug
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the difference between affinity and potency?

options.a: Affinity is the clinical effect produced while potency is the strength of receptor binding
options.b: Affinity is how well a drug binds to a receptor; potency is the dose needed for effect
options.c: Potency measures how tightly the drug binds to the receptor at its site
options.d: Affinity measures the size of the clinical effect the drug can produce

explanation:
Affinity (Kd): binding strength to receptor (measured in binding assays). Potency (EC50): concentration needed for 50% of maximum effect (functional assays). A high-affinity drug may have low potency if it has low intrinsic activity.

Additional: is the amount of drug needed to produce a given effect
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the chemical structure of penicillin G (benzylpenicillin)?

options.a: 6-APA with a benzyl side chain
options.b: Penicillin nucleus with a phenylacetamido
options.c: A cephalosporin structure
options.d: A macrolide structure

explanation:
Penicillin G: 6-phenylacetamidopenicillanic acid. It has the beta-lactam ring fused to thiazolidine ring, with a phenylacetamido group at C-6. Active against Gram-positive bacteria.

Note: beta-lactam + thiazolidine

Additional: side chain at position 6
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: Why is penicillin G acid-labile (destroyed in stomach acid)?

options.a: The thiazolidine ring becomes saturated and loses its sulfur atom in acid
options.b: The beta-lactam ring is susceptible to acid-catalyzed hydrolysis
options.c: The carboxyl group undergoes rapid decarboxylation in the acidic stomach
options.d: The molecule is destroyed by the high ionic strength of the gastric juice

explanation:
The beta-lactam ring is strained and susceptible to acid-catalyzed hydrolysis. Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen activates the ring toward nucleophilic attack by water, opening the lactam.

Additional: opened by protonation of the amide carbonyl
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: How were acid-stable penicillins developed?

options.a: By changing the thiazolidine ring
options.b: By introducing an electron-withdrawing group
options.c: By removing the beta-lactam ring
options.d: By adding more benzyl groups

explanation:
Penicillin V (phenoxymethylpenicillin) has an electron-withdrawing oxygen next to the amide nitrogen, which reduces the nucleophilicity of the amide nitrogen and decreases acid-catalyzed beta-lactam ring opening.

Note: reducing beta-lactam ring opening

Note: e.g., phenoxymethyl in penicillin V

Additional: adjacent to the amide nitrogen
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the role of the acyl side chain in penicillin activity?

options.a: It has no role
options.b: The side chain determines spectrum
options.c: It only affects solubility
options.d: It makes penicillin inactive

explanation:
The acyl side chain at C-6 determines: antibacterial spectrum (Gram-positive vs broad-spectrum), acid stability, beta-lactamase susceptibility, and protein binding.

Note: and resistance to beta-lactamase

Additional: of activity acid stability
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Vilsmeier-Haack reaction?

options.a: A hydrolysis reaction in which an ester is cleaved by dilute acid
options.b: A formylation reaction using DMF and POCl3 to introduce a formyl group
options.c: An oxidation reaction converting a primary alcohol into an aldehyde
options.d: A reduction reaction that converts a nitro group into an amino group

explanation:
Vilsmeier-Haack: DMF + POCl3 generates a chloroiminium ion that acts as an electrophile, introducing a formyl group (-CHO) on electron-rich aromatics and heterocycles.

Additional: introduce a -CHO group on electron-rich aromatic rings
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Sandmeyer reaction?

options.a: Reaction of an aromatic compound with concentrated sulfuric acid
options.b: Replacement of a diazonium group with -Cl, -Br
options.c: A reduction reaction applied to aromatic nitro compounds
options.d: A hydrolysis reaction in which an ester is cleaved by water

explanation:
Sandmeyer: Ar-N2+ + CuX → Ar-X (X = Cl, Br, CN). Aromatic diazonium salts are converted to aryl halides or nitriles using copper(I) chloride/bromide/cyanide.

Note: or -CN using copper(I) salts as catalysts
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Fries rearrangement?

options.a: A thermal rearrangement of alkyl groups between two aromatic rings
options.b: Lewis acid-catalyzed rearrangement of phenyl esters
options.c: A condensation reaction between two molecules of a phenol
options.d: A reduction reaction converting a ketone into a secondary alcohol

explanation:
Fries rearrangement: phenyl ester + AlCl3 → ortho- and para-acylphenols. Position of product depends on temperature (low temp favors para; high temp favors ortho).

Additional: to give ortho- and para-hydroxyaryl ketones
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of the oxazolidinone ring?

options.a: No significance
options.b: It is the pharmacophore of oxazolidinone
options.c: It is found in all antibiotics
options.d: It is a metabolite only

explanation:
The oxazolidinone ring (with a carbonyl at C-2 and substituents at C-5) is essential for the antibacterial activity of linezolid and tedizolid, which inhibit the 50S ribosomal subunit.

Additional: antibiotics that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis

question_text: What is the chemical structure of morphine?

options.a: A simple benzene derivative
options.b: A pentacyclic alkaloid with a phenanthrene core
options.c: A simple heterocyclic compound
options.d: A long-chain polymer built from repeating amino acid units

explanation:
Morphine is a pentacyclic (5 rings) opioid alkaloid: Ring A (aromatic), B (cyclohexane), C (cyclohexene), D (piperidine), E (dihydrofuran). Key groups: 3-OH, 6-OH, N-methyl, 4,5-epoxy bridge.

Note: A-E

Additional: containing five rings with key functional groups
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the SAR of morphine?

options.a: No structure-activity relationship has ever been established for morphine
options.b: 3-OH is essential; N-methyl can be replaced or removed
options.c: Only the basic nitrogen atom determines all of morphine's actions
options.d: Only the aromatic ring contributes to morphine's analgesic activity

explanation:
Morphine SAR: 3-OH essential for activity (methylation → codeine = prodrug); N-methyl → N-CH3 (naloxone: N-CH2CH=CH2 = antagonist); 6-OH removal → codeine; C-7,8 unsaturation affects potency.

Note: 5-epoxy bridge is important

Note: remove → codeine, less active

Additional: modified; 6-OH removal increases lipophilicity; 4
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the difference between morphine and naloxone structurally?

options.a: Both compounds carry identical substituents on the aromatic ring system
options.b: Morphine has an N-methyl group; naloxone has an allyl group at that position
options.c: Morphine carries an allyl group while naloxone carries an N-methyl group
options.d: Naloxone lacks the phenanthrene ring system entirely

explanation:
The N-substituent determines agonist/antagonist activity: N-methyl (morphine) = agonist. N-allyl/cyclopropylmethyl (naloxone/naltrexone) = antagonist. This is a key SAR finding in opioid chemistry.

Note: N-CH2CH=CH2

Additional: group which makes it an antagonist

Note: naloxone has N-allyl
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Beckett-Casy hypothesis for opioid receptor binding?

options.a: A model describing how opioids are absorbed across the intestinal wall into the blood
options.b: A model describing how opioids bind to receptors via aromatic and ionic interactions
options.c: A model of how opioids distribute into fatty tissue after intravenous injection
options.d: A model describing the renal excretion pathway of opioid metabolites

explanation:
Beckett-Casy: opioid activity requires 1) flat aromatic surface for receptor binding (Ring A), 2) quaternary/tertiary nitrogen for ionic interaction with receptor, 3) specific 3D arrangement (ethano bridge) for optimal fit.

Note: and ethylene bridge for correct spatial orientation

Note: aromatic ring for pi-stacking, tertiary nitrogen for ionic interaction
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the significance of the 3-OH group in morphine?

options.a: It mainly determines the bitter taste of the morphine molecule
options.b: The 3-OH group is essential for opioid activity — it forms hydrogen bonds with the receptor
options.c: It is the only group that allows morphine to form salts with acids
options.d: It must remain free for morphine to cross the blood-brain barrier

explanation:
The 3-OH (phenolic hydroxyl) forms hydrogen bonds with the opioid receptor. Methylation (codeine) reduces direct receptor binding ~10x. Codeine is demethylated to morphine in the liver (CYP2D6).

Note: as in codeine

Additional: blocking it reduces direct activity making codeine a prodrug
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Weerman degradation?

options.a: Conversion of alpha-hydroxy acids into their corresponding ketones
options.b: Conversion of alpha-hydroxy amides to aldehydes
options.c: A reaction that converts primary amines directly into carboxylic acids
options.d: A rearrangement that converts beta-hydroxy esters into amides

explanation:
Weerman degradation: R-CH(OH)-CONH2 + NaOCl → R-CHO + OCN-. Converts alpha-hydroxy amides to aldehydes with loss of the amide carbon.

Additional: aldehydes and isocyanates using hypochlorite
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Zincke reaction?

options.a: The reaction of zinc metal with dilute acids to liberate hydrogen gas
options.b: Ring-opening of pyridine with anilines followed by ring closure to give substituted pyridines
options.c: Catalytic reduction of the pyridine ring to piperidine using hydrogen
options.d: Oxidation of anilines to nitroso compounds using hydrogen peroxide

explanation:
Zincke reaction: pyridine ring opening with anilines (Zincke reagent = 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene) followed by ring closure to give N-arylpyridinium salts.

Additional: by reclosure to form N-arylpyridinium salts
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Hinsberg test?

options.a: A test for alcohols
options.b: A test to distinguish primary, secondary
options.c: A test for carboxylic acids
options.d: A test for aldehydes

explanation:
Hinsberg: benzenesulfonyl chloride + amine. Primary amines → sulfonamide soluble in NaOH. Secondary amines → sulfonamide insoluble. Tertiary amines → no reaction.

Note: and tertiary amines using benzenesulfonyl chloride
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the Hinsberg reagent?

options.a: Hydrochloric acid
options.b: Benzenesulfonyl chloride
options.c: Nitrous acid
options.d: Copper sulfate

explanation:
Hinsberg reagent is benzenesulfonyl chloride, which reacts with amines to form sulfonamides. The solubility properties of the product in NaOH distinguish primary from secondary amines.

Note: C6H5SO2Cl
subject: pharmaceutical-chemistry-i

question_text: What is the importance of prodrug design in overcoming the first-pass effect?

options.a: Prodrugs are always more water-soluble than their corresponding parent drugs
options.b: Lipophilic prodrugs may bypass gut wall metabolism, reducing first-pass loss
options.c: Prodrugs undergo more extensive gut wall metabolism than the active parent drug
options.d: Prodrug design cannot improve the oral absorption of poorly permeable drugs

explanation:
Prodrug strategies to overcome first-pass: 1) Lipophilic esters for better absorption. 2) Targeted activation at specific sites. 3) Avoiding CYP450 substrates. 4) Using alternative routes (sublingual, transdermal).

Additional: prodrugs can be designed for targeted activation

Note: certain

question_text: Pharmaceutical chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with:
options: Synthesis, analysis and standardization of drugs
Only the marketing of drug products
explanation: Pharmaceutical chemistry covers the synthesis, identification, analysis and standardization of medicinal substances.

question_text: A pharmacopoeia is best defined as:
options: An official book of standards for drugs
explanation: A pharmacopoeia is a legally recognized book containing standards of identity, purity and strength for drugs.

question_text: The Indian Pharmacopoeia is published under the authority of:
explanation: The Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, under the Ministry of Health, publishes the Indian Pharmacopoeia.

question_text: The first edition of the Indian Pharmacopoeia was published in:
explanation: The first edition of the Indian Pharmacopoeia was published in 1955; the current edition is IP 2022.

question_text: The National Formulary of India is primarily meant for:
options: Prescribing and dispensing information for official drugs
Fixing the maximum retail price of drugs
explanation: The NFI gives prescribing and dispensing information for drugs included in the pharmacopoeia.

question_text: In a pharmacopoeial monograph, the physical form and appearance of a drug is given under:
explanation: The 'Description' section in a monograph records color, odor, taste and physical form of the drug.

question_text: A drug is said to be 'official' when it:
options: Is included in the current pharmacopoeia
explanation: Official drugs are those whose standards are recognized in the current edition of the pharmacopoeia.

question_text: Impurities may enter pharmaceutical substances during:
options: Never, if the process is chemical
explanation: Impurities arise from raw materials, chemical processes, containers, atmospheric moisture and decomposition during storage.

question_text: Limit tests in pharmacopoeias are carried out to:
options: Check that impurities are within permissible limits
explanation: Limit tests compare the amount of an impurity with a standard, ensuring it does not exceed the permitted limit.

question_text: An assay of a pharmaceutical substance determines:
options: The amount of the active ingredient present
explanation: Assay is the quantitative estimation of the active principle in a drug sample by chemical or instrumental methods.

question_text: Systematic (determinate) errors in analysis are:
options: Reproducible errors due to faulty method or instruments
Errors caused only by careless reading
explanation: Systematic errors are constant and reproducible, caused by faulty calibration, impure reagents or method defects; they shift results in one direction.

question_text: Random (indeterminate) errors are characterized by:
options: Small unpredictable variations in replicate measurements
Errors that can be completely eliminated
Errors arising only from impure reagents
explanation: Random errors scatter results equally around the true value; they cannot be eliminated but are reduced by replicate determinations and statistics.

question_text: Accuracy of an analytical method refers to its:
options: Closeness of the measured value to the true value
explanation: Accuracy is the nearness of a result to the true value, whereas precision is the agreement between replicate measurements.

question_text: The number of significant figures in the value 0.00250 is:
explanation: Leading zeros are not significant; in 0.00250 the significant figures are 2, 5 and the trailing zero = 3.

question_text: Analytical reagent (AR) grade chemicals are used for:
explanation: AR grade reagents meet strict purity specifications and are used in quantitative analysis where impurities would interfere.

question_text: According to Arrhenius concept, an acid is a substance that:
options: Gives hydrogen ions in aqueous solution
Gives hydroxyl ions in aqueous solution
explanation: Arrhenius defined acids as substances that ionize in water to give H+ ions and bases as those giving OH− ions.

question_text: According to Lewis concept, an acid is defined as:
explanation: Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor and Lewis base is an electron-pair donor; this concept covers reactions without protons.

question_text: When sodium bicarbonate reacts with stomach hydrochloric acid, the gas liberated is:
explanation: NaHCO3 + HCl gives NaCl + H2O + CO2; the carbon dioxide causes belching, a drawback of bicarbonate antacids.

question_text: A buffer solution is one that:
options: Resists change in pH on adding small amounts of acid or base
Keeps a constant very low pH always
Has no acid or base in it
Changes color with every drop of acid
explanation: Buffers resist pH change by neutralizing added acid or base; they contain a weak acid with its salt or a weak base with its salt.

question_text: The buffer capacity of a buffer is maximum when:
options: The pH of the buffer equals the pKa of the weak acid
The buffer contains only the salt
The buffer contains only the weak acid
explanation: Buffer action is strongest at pH = pKa (equal concentrations of acid and salt), according to the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.

question_text: Phosphate buffer is commonly used in pharmaceuticals because it:
options: Maintains pH in the physiological range with low toxicity
explanation: Phosphate buffers effectively maintain pH near physiological values (about 7.4) and are well tolerated.

question_text: Methylparaben and propylparaben are often used together as preservatives because the combination:
options: Gives a broader spectrum of antimicrobial activity
explanation: Mixing methyl and propyl parabens widens the antimicrobial spectrum and improves effectiveness across pH ranges.

question_text: EDTA (disodium edetate) is added to pharmaceutical formulations to:
options: Bind metal ions that catalyze oxidative degradation
Increase the pH of the solution
Improve the taste of the syrup
explanation: EDTA chelates trace metal ions (Fe, Cu) that catalyze oxidation, thereby stabilizing the formulation.

question_text: Antioxidants are added to pharmaceutical preparations to:
options: Prevent oxidative deterioration of the active drug
Increase the rate of drug absorption
Mask the bitter taste of drugs
explanation: Antioxidants such as sodium metabisulphite and BHA prevent oxidation of easily oxidizable drugs like adrenaline and ascorbic acid.

question_text: Dilute hydrochloric acid is used in medicine as:
explanation: Dilute HCl is given orally as an acidifying agent when gastric acid secretion is deficient (achlorhydria).

question_text: An alkalizing agent used to correct systemic acidosis is:
explanation: Sodium bicarbonate is an alkalizing agent that raises blood pH and corrects metabolic acidosis.

question_text: Buffers are incorporated into ophthalmic solutions mainly to:
options: Maintain physiological pH and avoid eye irritation
explanation: Ophthalmic solutions are buffered near tear pH (about 7.4) to prevent stinging and damage to the cornea.

question_text: An acidic buffer is prepared from:
options: A weak acid and its salt with a strong base
A strong acid and a strong base
A weak base and its salt with a strong acid
explanation: Acidic buffers (pH below 7) contain a weak acid with its salt, e.g., acetic acid with sodium acetate.

question_text: Phenol in small concentration is used as a preservative in:
options: Injections such as insulin and some vaccines
explanation: Phenol (about 0.5%) is used to preserve multidose injections like insulin where other preservatives are unsuitable.

question_text: An example of a basic (alkaline) buffer used in pharmacy is:
explanation: Ammonia-ammonium chloride forms a basic buffer (pH above 7); the others listed are acidic buffers.

question_text: The main disadvantage of sodium bicarbonate as an antacid is:
explanation: Sodium bicarbonate reacts rapidly, liberating CO2 and can cause acid rebound and systemic alkalosis on absorption.

question_text: Aluminium hydroxide gel commonly causes which side effect?
explanation: Aluminium hydroxide is constipating because aluminium ions slow intestinal motility; hence it is combined with magnesium hydroxide.

question_text: Magnesium hydroxide suspension is commonly known as:
explanation: Milk of magnesia is the aqueous suspension of magnesium hydroxide used as an antacid and laxative.

question_text: Aluminium hydroxide is combined with magnesium hydroxide in antacid preparations to:
options: Balance the bowel effects of the two antacids
Increase the cost of the product
explanation: Aluminium causes constipation while magnesium causes diarrhea; the combination gives a balanced laxative effect.

question_text: Calcium carbonate used as an antacid produces:
options: Carbon dioxide gas with possible acid rebound
explanation: CaCO3 reacts with HCl liberating CO2 (belching) and absorbed calcium may cause acid rebound and hypercalcemia.

question_text: Bismuth salts are used in gastrointestinal disorders because of their:
options: Astringent and protective action in diarrhea
explanation: Bismuth subcarbonate/subsalicylate coat and protect the gut mucosa with astringent and mild antibacterial action.

question_text: A saline (osmotic) cathartic acts by:
options: Retaining water in the intestine by osmosis
Absorbing all water from the gut
explanation: Saline cathartics like magnesium sulphate are poorly absorbed and hold water in the gut by osmosis, increasing bulk and stimulating evacuation.

question_text: Epsom salt is the common pharmaceutical name of:
explanation: Epsom salt is hydrated magnesium sulphate (MgSO4·7H2O), used as a saline purgative and in magnesium deficiency.

question_text: Light kaolin is chemically:
explanation: Kaolin is a native hydrated aluminium silicate (Al2O3·2SiO2·2H2O) used as an adsorbent in diarrhea.

question_text: Activated charcoal differs from ordinary charcoal mainly because it:
options: Has a much larger adsorptive surface area
explanation: Activation creates countless micropores, hugely increasing the surface area available for adsorbing poisons.

question_text: Pectin is included in antidiarrheal mixtures because it:
options: Acts as a demulcent and adsorbent
explanation: Pectin, a vegetable colloid, coats the intestinal mucosa (demulcent) and adsorbs toxins and water in diarrhea.

question_text: Insoluble antacids such as aluminium hydroxide are preferred over soluble antacids because they:
options: Act much faster on an empty stomach
Are completely excreted by the lungs
explanation: Non-absorbable antacids act locally in the gut without entering the circulation, avoiding systemic electrolyte disturbance.

question_text: Simethicone is added to antacid preparations to:
explanation: Simethicone is a silicone defoaming agent that breaks gas bubbles in the gut, relieving bloating and flatulence.

question_text: An acidifying agent used in the treatment of achlorhydria is:
explanation: Dilute HCl replaces deficient gastric acid in achlorhydria and aids digestion and iron absorption.

question_text: The laxative that acts by lubricating the intestinal contents is:
explanation: Liquid paraffin is a mineral oil that coats the stool and gut, lubricating passage without stimulating peristalsis.

question_text: An antiseptic is an agent that:
options: Prevents the growth of microorganisms on living tissues
Destroys microbes only on inanimate objects
Kills all bacteria in the bloodstream
Is used exclusively for sterilizing surgical instruments
explanation: Antiseptics are applied to living tissue (skin, mucous membrane) to inhibit microbial growth; disinfectants are used on inanimate surfaces.

question_text: A disinfectant is an agent that:
options: Is applied to living tissues only
Has no antimicrobial action at all
explanation: Disinfectants are strong antimicrobials used on floors, instruments and other inanimate objects; they are generally too irritant for tissues.

question_text: Zinc sulphate is used in eye lotions mainly as:
explanation: Zinc sulphate has mild astringent and antiseptic action and is used in eye lotions for conjunctivitis.

question_text: Calamine is chemically a:
options: Zinc carbonate with a small amount of ferric oxide
Purified zinc oxide free from any colorant
Magnesium silicate with ferric oxide tint
explanation: Calamine is zinc carbonate colored pink by a small proportion of ferric oxide; it is soothing in skin lotions.

question_text: Zinc oxide ointment is commonly used for:
options: Protecting skin in diaper rash and minor wounds
explanation: Zinc oxide is a mild astringent, protective and soothing agent used in diaper rash, eczema and minor skin irritation.

question_text: Hydrogen peroxide solution must be stored in:
options: Amber colored bottles away from light and heat
Clear glass bottles in direct sunlight
explanation: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes in light and heat to water and oxygen, so it is kept in amber bottles in a cool place.

question_text: Iodine is dissolved in water with the help of:
explanation: Iodine is almost insoluble in water; adding potassium iodide forms soluble triiodide, allowing aqueous iodine solutions.

question_text: Povidone-iodine is preferred over tincture iodine because it:
options: Is less irritating and releases iodine slowly
Cannot be used on the skin
explanation: Povidone-iodine complex releases free iodine slowly with less irritation and staining than alcoholic tincture of iodine.

question_text: Tincture of iodine contains iodine along with:
explanation: Tincture of iodine is an alcoholic solution of iodine with potassium iodide (about 2% iodine).

question_text: Silver nitrate in the form of toughened sticks is used for:
options: Removing warts and cauterizing small lesions
explanation: Silver nitrate sticks cauterize warts, ulcers and hypergranulation tissue by precipitating tissue proteins.

question_text: Chlorinated lime is used as:
options: A disinfectant for water and wounds
explanation: Chlorinated lime (bleaching powder) releases chlorine and is used to disinfect water, drains and wounds.

question_text: Sodium hypochlorite solution is used as a:
explanation: Sodium hypochlorite (bleach) is a powerful disinfectant that also bleaches, and is used at low strength in wound care.

question_text: Formaldehyde solution (formalin) is used as:
options: A disinfectant and preservative of biological specimens
A local anesthetic for surface use
explanation: Formalin (about 40% formaldehyde) disinfects instruments and preserves anatomical and biological specimens.

question_text: 20 volume hydrogen peroxide means that 1 mL of the solution liberates:
explanation: The 'volume strength' states the volume of oxygen gas released by one volume of the solution; 20 volume gives 20 mL O2 per mL.

question_text: An ideal antiseptic should be:
explanation: A good antiseptic acts rapidly, is effective against many organisms, is non-irritating, stable and safe on tissues.

question_text: Fluoride prevents dental caries by:
options: Making tooth enamel more resistant to acid attack
explanation: Fluoride converts hydroxyapatite to less soluble fluorapatite and promotes remineralization, making enamel acid-resistant.

question_text: The recommended level of fluoride in community drinking water is about:
explanation: Water fluoridation at about 0.7-1.0 ppm reduces caries while avoiding fluorosis; higher levels cause mottling.

question_text: Stannous fluoride is commonly used as:
explanation: Stannous (tin) fluoride is an effective anticaries fluoride used in dentifrices and topical gels.

question_text: Sodium monofluorophosphate is incorporated in toothpastes as:
options: A source of fluoride for caries prevention
explanation: Sodium monofluorophosphate slowly releases fluoride in the mouth, providing anticaries action in dentifrices.

question_text: Excessive intake of fluoride during tooth formation causes:
explanation: High fluoride intake during enamel formation produces mottled, discolored teeth (dental fluorosis).

question_text: Dental fluorosis develops when excess fluoride is ingested during:
options: Old age after teeth have erupted
explanation: Fluorosis occurs only while teeth are forming (up to about 8 years of age); mature enamel is unaffected.

question_text: The fluoride concentration in most anticaries toothpastes is about:
explanation: Standard fluoride toothpastes contain about 1000-1500 ppm fluoride for effective caries prevention.

question_text: Silver diamine fluoride is used in dentistry to:
explanation: Silver diamine fluoride arrests active caries by combining antibacterial silver with remineralizing fluoride.

question_text: Topical fluoride application by a dentist is recommended mainly for:
options: Prevention of dental caries in high-risk patients
explanation: Professional topical fluoride (gel, varnish or rinse) is applied to prevent caries in children and high-risk adults.

question_text: Fluoride inhibits the growth of cariogenic bacteria by:
options: Interfering with bacterial enolase and acid production
explanation: Fluoride inhibits enolase in bacteria, reducing acid production that causes demineralization of enamel.

question_text: Acute fluoride poisoning can be treated by administering:
explanation: Calcium (as calcium gluconate or milk) precipitates fluoride as insoluble calcium fluoride and is the emergency treatment.

question_text: Zinc chloride is used in mouthwash preparations as:
explanation: Zinc chloride has astringent and mild antiseptic properties used in mouthwashes and gingival applications.

question_text: Potassium nitrate is added to desensitizing toothpastes to:
options: Block pain transmission in dentinal nerves
explanation: Potassium nitrate penetrates dentinal tubules and reduces nerve excitability, relieving dentine hypersensitivity.

question_text: Strontium chloride is used in dentifrices for:
explanation: Strontium salts occlude dentinal tubules, reducing the sensitivity of exposed dentine.

question_text: Dilute hydrogen peroxide is used in mouthwashes as:
options: An oral antiseptic and cleansing agent
explanation: Dilute hydrogen peroxide releases oxygen and acts as a mild antiseptic and cleansing agent in oral care.

question_text: Ammonium chloride acts as an expectorant by:
options: Reflexly stimulating bronchial secretions through gastric irritation
explanation: Ammonium chloride irritates the gastric mucosa, reflexly increasing bronchial secretion and thinning mucus (expectorant action).

question_text: Potassium iodide is used in respiratory medicine as:
explanation: Potassium iodide increases respiratory secretions, acting as a stimulant expectorant in chronic bronchitis.

question_text: Iron is absorbed best in the:
options: Any form equally from the stomach
explanation: Only ferrous iron is absorbed, chiefly in the duodenum and upper jejunum; ferric iron must be reduced first.

question_text: A common side effect of oral ferrous sulphate therapy is:
explanation: Oral iron commonly causes nausea, epigastric pain, constipation (with black stools); taken after food it is better tolerated.

question_text: Iron deficiency anemia is treated with:
options: Oral ferrous salts such as ferrous sulphate
explanation: Oral ferrous salts are first-line for iron deficiency anemia; parenteral iron is reserved for intolerance or malabsorption.

question_text: Ascorbic acid is given along with oral iron preparations because it:
options: Reduces ferric iron to the absorbable ferrous form
Increases the taste of the syrup
Decreases the acidity of the stomach
explanation: Vitamin C keeps iron in the ferrous state and forms soluble complexes, improving its absorption from the gut.

question_text: Activated charcoal is most effective in poisoning when given:
options: Soon after the poison is ingested
After the poison has been fully absorbed
Only when the patient is unconscious
explanation: Activated charcoal adsorbs poison in the gut, so it must be given early (within 1-2 hours) before absorption is complete.

question_text: The specific antidote for cyanide poisoning is:
explanation: Cyanide poisoning is treated with amyl nitrite and sodium nitrite (forming methaemoglobin) followed by sodium thiosulphate to form thiocyanate.

question_text: Calcium disodium edetate is the specific antidote for:
explanation: Calcium disodium edetate chelates lead and increases its urinary excretion in lead poisoning.

question_text: Dimercaprol (BAL) is used as the antidote for poisoning with:
explanation: Dimercaprol (British Anti-Lewisite) chelates arsenic, mercury and gold, increasing their excretion.

question_text: Methylene blue is used as an antidote for:
explanation: Methylene blue reduces methaemoglobin back to hemoglobin and is used in nitrate/nitrite induced methaemoglobinaemia.

question_text: Potassium permanganate is used in poisoning as:
options: An oxidizing agent for gastric lavage
explanation: Dilute potassium permanganate oxidizes and inactivates many poisons (e.g., alkaloids, cyanide) when used for gastric lavage.

question_text: The specific antidote for iron poisoning is:
explanation: Deferoxamine chelates ferric iron and is given parenterally in acute iron poisoning.

question_text: Ferrous fumarate is preferred over ferrous sulphate by some patients because it:
options: Contains more elemental iron with less gastric irritation
Is completely free of any side effects
Does not need to be swallowed
explanation: Ferrous fumarate has a higher elemental iron content (about 33%) and is generally better tolerated.

question_text: Antidotes act by all of the following mechanisms EXCEPT:
options: Enhancing the absorption of the poison
explanation: Antidotes work by chemical neutralization, chelation, pharmacological antagonism or reducing absorption, never by enhancing poison absorption.

question_text: Ringer's solution contains:
options: Sodium, potassium and calcium chlorides in water
explanation: Ringer's solution contains NaCl, KCl and CaCl2 in distilled water, replacing extracellular fluid electrolytes.

question_text: Dextrose (glucose) saline infusion is used to:
explanation: Dextrose saline supplies water, electrolytes and calories in dehydration and energy deficit states.

question_text: Potassium is the main cation of:
explanation: Potassium is the principal intracellular cation, whereas sodium dominates extracellular fluid.

question_text: Hypokalemia is treated by giving:
explanation: Oral or IV potassium chloride replaces the potassium deficit in hypokalemia caused by diuretics or diarrhea.

question_text: Calcium gluconate is preferred over calcium chloride for intravenous use because it:
options: Causes less tissue necrosis if extravasated
Acts much faster on the heart
explanation: Calcium chloride is highly irritating and causes severe tissue necrosis on leakage, so the less irritant gluconate is used IV.

question_text: Calcium ions are essential for all of the following EXCEPT:
explanation: Calcium is needed for clotting, muscle contraction, nerve transmission and bone formation, but intracellular K+ balance is not its role.

question_text: The WHO-recommended ORS contains sodium chloride, potassium chloride, glucose and:
explanation: Low-osmolarity WHO-ORS contains NaCl, KCl, glucose and trisodium citrate dihydrate (citrate replaces the older bicarbonate).

question_text: Zinc is now added to ORS because it:
options: Reduces the duration and severity of diarrhea
Prevents the growth of bacteria in the packet
Increases the shelf life of the sachet
explanation: Zinc supplementation (14 days) shortens the duration of diarrhea and prevents further episodes, especially in children.

question_text: Sodium bicarbonate injection is used to correct:
explanation: IV sodium bicarbonate raises blood pH and is used in severe metabolic acidosis (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis, cardiac arrest).

question_text: Magnesium sulphate injection is used in the management of:
explanation: IV magnesium sulphate is the drug of choice to prevent and treat seizures in severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia.

question_text: Ammonium chloride given systemically acts as:
explanation: Ammonium chloride is converted to urea in the liver releasing H+, acidifying the body; it is used in metabolic alkalosis.

question_text: Calcium lactate is used therapeutically as:
explanation: Calcium lactate is a well-tolerated oral calcium salt used in calcium deficiency states.

question_text: Intravenous fluids for clinical use must be:
explanation: IV fluids must be sterile and pyrogen-free; isotonicity prevents hemolysis or cell shrinkage on infusion.

question_text: Normal saline is an isotonic solution containing:
explanation: Normal saline is 0.9% w/v NaCl, isotonic with plasma and used for fluid and electrolyte replacement.

question_text: Hypertonic saline (3-5% NaCl) is used clinically for:
explanation: Hypertonic saline corrects dangerously low serum sodium (symptomatic hyponatremia) and cerebral edema.

question_text: Barium sulphate is used as an X-ray contrast agent for imaging the:
explanation: Barium sulphate is given orally (barium meal) or rectally (barium enema) to outline the gastrointestinal tract on X-rays.

question_text: Barium sulphate is safe for oral administration because it is:
options: Practically insoluble in water and body fluids
explanation: Barium sulphate is insoluble, so it is not absorbed; soluble barium salts are highly toxic and must be absent.

question_text: Iodinated contrast media are used in radiology for:
explanation: Water-soluble iodinated contrast agents opacity blood vessels and the urinary tract in angiography and IVU/CT scans.

question_text: Radiopharmaceuticals are substances used in medicine for:
options: Diagnosis and therapy using radioactive isotopes
explanation: Radiopharmaceuticals carry a radioisotope for imaging (diagnosis) or targeted radiation (therapy), e.g., in nuclear medicine.

question_text: Technetium-99m is widely used in nuclear imaging because it:
options: Has a short half-life and suitable gamma energy
explanation: Tc-99m emits gamma rays of ideal energy with a 6-hour half-life, giving good images at low radiation dose.

question_text: Iodine-131 is used in nuclear medicine for:
explanation: I-131 concentrates in the thyroid, so it is used to image and treat thyroid disorders including hyperthyroidism and thyroid cancer.

question_text: An ideal X-ray contrast agent should be:
explanation: Contrast media must be safe, absorb X-rays well and be excreted promptly without leaving residues.

question_text: Barium sulphate used for X-ray must be free from:
options: Soluble barium salts which are toxic
explanation: Soluble barium compounds are poisonous (cardiac and muscle toxicity); official barium sulphate is tested for their absence.

question_text: Lugol's iodine solution contains:
options: Iodine with potassium iodide in water
explanation: Lugol's iodine is 5% iodine with 10% potassium iodide in water, used in thyroid disorders and as a reagent.

question_text: Sodium iodide is used therapeutically in:
options: Thyroid disorders and as an expectorant
explanation: Sodium iodide is used in thyroid conditions (e.g., in thyrotoxic crisis with Lugol's iodine) and as an expectorant.

question_text: Non-ionic contrast media are preferred over ionic media because they:
options: Cause fewer allergic and adverse reactions
explanation: Non-ionic low-osmolality contrast agents are better tolerated with fewer hypersensitivity and hemodynamic effects.

question_text: A 'positive' X-ray contrast medium appears white on the film because it:
explanation: Positive contrast agents contain heavy atoms (barium, iodine) that absorb X-rays, casting a white shadow on the radiograph.

question_text: Air and carbon dioxide are examples of:
options: Negative contrast media that appear dark
Positive contrast media that appear white
explanation: Gases are negative contrast agents because they are radiolucent (absorb few X-rays) and appear dark on the film.

question_text: A patient allergic to iodine may react to:
explanation: Iodinated contrast agents can trigger allergic-type reactions in iodine-sensitive patients, ranging from rashes to anaphylaxis.

question_text: Premedication with antihistamines and steroids before contrast studies is done to:
options: Prevent anaphylactoid reactions to the contrast
Speed up excretion of the dye
explanation: At-risk patients receive antihistamines and corticosteroids before iodinated contrast to reduce the risk of allergic reactions.

question_text: The limit test for arsenic is carried out using the:
explanation: Arsenic is detected by the Gutzeit test, where arsine gas produces a yellow to brown stain on mercuric chloride paper.

question_text: In the Gutzeit test, arsenic is detected by the formation of a:
options: Brown stain on mercuric chloride paper
Blue color in the aqueous layer
explanation: Arsine (AsH3) reacts with mercuric chloride paper producing a yellowish-brown stain; intensity is compared with a standard.

question_text: The limit test for heavy metals compares the color produced with:
options: A standard lead solution treated with hydrogen sulfide
A standard sulphate solution treated with barium chloride
A standard arsenic solution treated with hydrogen sulfide
A dilute ferric chloride solution matched against iron standard
explanation: Heavy metals are precipitated as sulfides by thioacetamide/H2S at pH 3.5 and the brown color is compared with a lead standard.

question_text: Nessler's reagent is used in the limit test for:
explanation: Nessler's reagent (alkaline potassium mercuric iodide) gives a yellow-brown color with ammonia, used in the limit test for ammonium.

question_text: The limit test for iron is based on the color produced by iron with:
explanation: Ferric iron reacts with thioglycollic acid in ammoniacal citric acid solution to give a pink color compared with a standard.

question_text: Which of the following is a suitable primary standard substance?
explanation: Potassium hydrogen phthalate is a pure, stable, non-hygroscopic primary standard used to standardize alkalis.

question_text: A secondary standard solution is standardized against:
explanation: Secondary standards (e.g., NaOH, HCl of exact strength) are standardized by titrating against primary standards.

question_text: Normality of a solution is defined as the number of:
options: Gram equivalents of solute per liter of solution
Gram moles of solute per liter of solution
Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
explanation: Normality (N) = gram equivalent weight of solute per liter of solution; it depends on the reaction involved.

question_text: Molality of a solution is expressed as:
options: Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
Moles of solute per liter of solution
explanation: Molality (m) = moles of solute dissolved in one kilogram of solvent, independent of temperature.

question_text: The equivalent weight of anhydrous sodium carbonate (Na2CO3, MW 106) is:
explanation: Sodium carbonate reacts with 2 equivalents of acid, so equivalent weight = molecular weight / 2 = 106/2 = 53.

question_text: In the limit test for chloride, the opalescence produced is compared with:
options: A standard chloride solution treated with silver nitrate
A standard chloride solution treated with dilute ammonia
A standard sulphate solution treated with barium nitrate
A standard lead solution treated with hydrogen sulfide
explanation: Chloride reacts with silver nitrate in nitric acid to form opalescent silver chloride, matched against a standard chloride.

question_text: Nessler cylinders are used in limit tests for:
options: Comparing the turbidity or color of test and standard solutions
Measuring the exact volume of gas liberated in a reaction
Determining the weight of precipitate formed after filtration
Heating samples at controlled temperature for ignition
explanation: Nessler cylinders are matched glass tubes of equal bore used to visually compare turbidity or color in limit tests.

question_text: Loss on ignition of a substance mainly indicates:
options: Volatile matter and water of crystallization
Total ash and acid-insoluble ash content of the sample
The amount of organic impurities present in the substance
Its refractive index and optical rotation value
explanation: Loss on ignition measures material lost on strong heating, i.e., moisture, volatile matter and water of crystallization.

question_text: Volumetric (titrimetric) analysis is based on the measurement of:
options: The volume of a reagent solution that reacts with the analyte
The weight of the precipitate formed
The color intensity of the solution
The light absorbed by the sample
explanation: Volumetric analysis measures the volume of a standard reagent needed to react completely with a measured amount of analyte.

question_text: In limit tests, the term 'limit' refers to:
options: The maximum permissible amount of an impurity
The minimum dose of the drug
The expiry period of the reagent
The volume of the sample taken
explanation: The limit is the maximum quantity of an impurity allowed in the official substance; results are compared as 'not more than' the standard.

question_text: In a titration, the equivalence point is:
options: The point where acid and base are stoichiometrically equivalent
The point where the color changes permanently
The midpoint of the burette reading
Always at pH 7 for every titration
explanation: The equivalence point is when the added titrant is chemically equivalent to the analyte; the endpoint is where the indicator changes color.

question_text: An acid-base indicator is a substance that:
options: Shows the endpoint by a sharp color change
Participates in the chemical reaction fully
Increases the speed of the reaction
explanation: Indicators are weak acids/bases whose color differs in ionized and unionized forms, signaling the endpoint.

question_text: The most suitable indicator for titration of a strong acid with a weak base is:
explanation: The equivalence point of strong acid-weak base is acidic (pH below 7), so an indicator changing in the acidic range like methyl orange is used.

question_text: The most suitable indicator for titration of a weak acid with a strong base is:
explanation: The equivalence point of weak acid-strong base is alkaline (pH above 7), so phenolphthalein (range 8.2-10) is chosen.

question_text: The pH at the equivalence point of a strong acid and weak base titration is:
explanation: The salt formed (e.g., NH4Cl) hydrolyzes to give an acidic solution, so the equivalence pH is below 7.

question_text: The pH at the equivalence point of a weak acid and strong base titration is:
explanation: The salt (e.g., sodium acetate) hydrolyzes to produce a basic solution, so the equivalence pH is above 7.

question_text: Methyl red indicator changes color in the pH range:
explanation: Methyl red changes from red to yellow between pH 4.2 and 6.3, used for strong acid-weak base titrations.

question_text: Complexometric titration using EDTA is commonly employed to estimate:
explanation: EDTA forms stable complexes with metal ions; complexometric titrations estimate Ca, Mg, Zn, Al etc., including water hardness.

question_text: Murexide is used as the indicator in the EDTA titration of:
explanation: Murexide (ammonium purpurate) gives a pink to purple end point when titrating calcium with EDTA.

question_text: Eriochrome black T is the indicator used in the EDTA titration of:
explanation: Eriochrome black T changes wine-red to blue at the endpoint in EDTA titration of magnesium and total hardness.

question_text: An example of a redox titration is the estimation of ferrous iron using:
options: Potassium permanganate or ceric ammonium sulphate
Complexometric titration using disodium EDTA solution
Precipitation titration employing silver nitrate reagent
Acid-base titration using standard sodium hydroxide
explanation: Ferrous iron is oxidized by potassium permanganate (permanganometry) or ceric sulphate (cerimetry) in redox titrations.

question_text: In permanganate titrations, potassium permanganate acts as its own indicator because:
options: The first excess of permanganate gives a pink color
It forms a blue precipitate at the end
explanation: Permanganate is deeply colored; after the endpoint no permanganate is consumed, so its pink color persists (self-indicating).

question_text: Oxalic acid is commonly used to standardize:
explanation: Sodium oxalate or oxalic acid is a primary standard used to standardize potassium permanganate in acid medium.

question_text: Mohr's method (precipitation titration) uses silver nitrate to estimate:
options: Chloride ions with potassium chromate indicator
explanation: In Mohr's method, chloride is titrated with silver nitrate using potassium chromate; the red silver chromate signals the endpoint.

question_text: Kjeldahl's method is used for the estimation of:
explanation: Kjeldahl digestion converts organic nitrogen to ammonium sulphate, which is distilled and titrated to estimate nitrogen/protein.

question_text: Chromatography is a technique used for:
options: Separating mixture components by differential distribution between two phases
Determining the melting point of solid substances accurately
Measuring the density of liquids by specific gravity bottle
Weighing precipitates with the help of an analytical balance
explanation: Chromatography separates components based on their different distribution between a stationary phase and a moving mobile phase.

question_text: In paper chromatography, the stationary phase is:
options: Water held by the cellulose fibers of the paper
explanation: Paper holds adsorbed water as the stationary phase; the developing solvent moves over it as the mobile phase (partition chromatography).

question_text: The adsorbent commonly used to coat TLC plates is:
explanation: Silica gel G (with calcium sulfate binder) is the most common adsorbent for thin layer chromatography plates.

question_text: Adsorption chromatography separates components according to their:
options: Different degrees of adsorption on the stationary phase
Their different solubilities in two immiscible solvents only
Their different partition between moving and stationary liquid phases
The different colors they develop with iodine vapor only
explanation: In adsorption chromatography, components with weaker adsorption move faster while strongly adsorbed ones are retained longer.

question_text: Partition chromatography is based on the:
options: Differential partitioning of solutes between two liquid phases
Adsorption of solutes on a solid surface
explanation: Partition chromatography separates by the different solubility/distribution of each component between the stationary liquid and the mobile phase.

question_text: Gas chromatography is mainly used for the analysis of:
options: Volatile compounds that can be vaporized without decomposition
High-boiling non-volatile salts and inorganic metal complexes
Heat-labile protein and enzyme molecules in biological fluids
Water-insoluble polymer materials of high molecular weight
explanation: GC requires samples to be volatile and thermally stable so they can be carried through the column in the gas phase.

question_text: In gas chromatography, the mobile phase is:
options: A carrier gas such as nitrogen or helium
explanation: An inert carrier gas (N2, He) transports vaporized sample components through the GC column.

question_text: The most common detectors used in HPLC are:
explanation: HPLC usually uses UV-visible absorbance or refractive index detection to measure eluted compounds.

question_text: HPLC is preferred over gas chromatography for:
explanation: HPLC works at ambient temperature with liquid mobile phases, so it suits non-volatile and thermolabile drugs.

question_text: In reverse-phase HPLC, the stationary phase is:
explanation: Reverse phase uses a non-polar stationary phase (C18/C8 silica) with a polar mobile phase like methanol-water.

question_text: Retention time in chromatography is defined as:
options: The time a component takes to travel through the column to the detector
The time the sample is heated before injection
The total time of the whole analysis day
The time the solvent bottle is left open
explanation: Retention time (tR) is the time from injection until the component peak appears at the detector; it aids identification.

question_text: Ion-exchange chromatography separates substances on the basis of their:
options: Ionic charge and affinity for the resin
explanation: Ion-exchange resins carry charged groups that reversibly bind oppositely charged ions, separating them by charge and affinity.

question_text: Gel filtration (size exclusion) chromatography separates molecules according to their:
explanation: Gel filtration uses porous beads; small molecules enter pores and are delayed, while large molecules elute first.

question_text: Thin layer chromatography is widely used in pharmaceutical analysis for:
options: Checking the purity and identity of drugs
explanation: TLC is a rapid, inexpensive method to check drug purity, identify compounds and monitor reactions.

question_text: The sample spot applied on a TLC plate should be:
options: Small and placed above the solvent level
Large and touching the solvent surface
Spread across the whole plate width
explanation: A compact spot is applied above the solvent level so the mobile phase can rise through it without dissolving the spot prematurely.
